title: The edge of life: deciding whether a tricky case is alive

summary.text: A candle flame moves, grows, takes in air and lights new flames, yet scientists say it is not alive. A dry seed does none of these things, yet they are alive. In this unit you test tricky cases against the signs of life: fire, a salt crystal, a robot, a dry seed, a tiny animal called a water bear, and a virus. You find that a flame and your own cells do the same chemistry, and that a crystal grows only by adding salt to its outside. Scientists still argue about viruses, and nobody yet knows how life first began.
summary.art: A kitchen table with a row of tricky cases: a candle flame, a salt crystal, a dry seed, a tiny eight-legged water bear, a toy robot and a spiky virus ball, and a child with a magnifying glass and a checklist.

intro.hook: A candle flame moves. It grows. It needs air, and it can light a new flame. A dry seed does none of these things. Yet scientists say the seed is alive and the flame is not. Why?
intro.text: In this unit you test six puzzling things against the signs of life: fire, a salt crystal, a robot, a dry seed, a tiny animal called a water bear, and a virus. Each one shows some signs and lacks others. By the end you will know which signs matter most, and why scientists still argue about where life begins.
intro.art: A lit candle on a steel plate next to a dry moong seed on an open palm, with a big question mark between them.
intro.context: This is the way into the unit: a puzzle about what makes a thing alive.

outcomes: I can test a tricky case against the signs of life, and say which signs it shows and which it lacks.
I can explain why fire and crystals show some signs of life but are not alive, and how my cells do the same chemistry as a flame, only slowly.
I can explain that a dry seed or a dried-out water bear is alive but resting, and show it with a seed test.
I can say what a virus is, and why scientists still argue about whether they are alive.
I can explain why a robot that moves and senses is not alive, and say what it lacks.
I can run a fair test with a comparison, such as seeds next to pebbles, and finish with claim, evidence and reasoning.
I can say why the edge between living and non-living is hard to draw, and that nobody yet knows how life began.

terms.meaning: Something that is alive. They are made of one or more cells. They take in food, use energy, grow, sense, get rid of waste and make more of their own kind.
terms.example: A neem tree, a cow, an ant, a mushroom and you are all living things.
terms.art: A neem tree, a cow, an ant, a mushroom and a child standing in a row.

terms.meaning: Something that is not alive and never was. It does not take in food or grow from inside.
terms.example: A stone, a steel spoon and the air are non-living.
terms.art: A stone, a steel spoon and a puff of air drawn as swirls.

terms.meaning: Something that was part of a living thing, but is not alive any more.
terms.example: A wooden table, a cotton shirt and a dry leaf were once parts of living things.
terms.art: A wooden table with a faint tree drawn behind it, a cotton shirt with a cotton plant behind it.

terms.meaning: The things living things do. Scientists usually list seven: taking in food, getting energy from food (respiration), growing, moving, sensing, getting rid of waste, and making young.
terms.example: A puppy moves, eats, grows and senses your hand. They show all the signs.
terms.art: Seven small pictures in a circle: a moving leg, a breath, an eye, a growing sprout, a baby, a waste bin and a plate of food.

terms.meaning: The tiny building block every living thing is made of. Most cells are far too small to see without a microscope.
terms.example: Your body is made of about 30 trillion cells. A bacterium is just one cell.
terms.art: A zoom circle on a child's arm showing a carpet of tiny round cells.

terms.meaning: The plan inside every cell that says how to build and run the living thing. Parents pass copies of it to their young.
terms.example: A mango seed has mango instructions inside, so they grow a mango tree, not a coconut palm.
terms.art: A mango seed with a tiny glowing instruction scroll inside, and a mango tree growing from the seed.

terms.meaning: How living things get energy from food. Inside cells, food joins with oxygen. This lets out energy, carbon dioxide gas and water.
terms.example: Your cells are doing respiration right now. The air you breathe out carries the carbon dioxide away.
terms.art: A child breathing out a misty puff onto a cold steel plate.

terms.meaning: Alive but resting. A dormant thing's life processes slow down so much that they seem to do nothing. They wake up when conditions are right.
terms.example: A dry karamani (cowpea) seed in the kitchen jar is dormant. Put them on wet cotton and they wake.
terms.art: A jar of dry karamani seeds with tiny sleeping eyes drawn on them.

terms.meaning: When a seed wakes up and starts to grow a root and a shoot.
terms.example: Soaked moong seeds germinate in a day or two. That is how sprouts are made.
terms.art: A moong seed splitting, with a white root curling out.

terms.meaning: A tiny animal with eight stubby legs, about half a millimetre long. They live in damp moss all over the world, even on city walls.
terms.example: Water bears can dry out completely, wait for years, and wake up when water comes back.
terms.art: A chubby eight-legged water bear climbing a strand of green moss, drawn very big.

terms.meaning: The dry, curled-up ball a water bear turns into when their home dries out. Their life almost stops.
terms.example: A tun can be blown about by the wind, then wake up in a rain puddle.
terms.art: A water bear curled into a tiny wrinkled barrel shape, like a dried pea.

terms.meaning: A solid whose tiny particles are lined up in a neat repeating pattern. Crystals grow by adding more particles on the outside.
terms.example: Salt grains, sugar grains and snowflakes are crystals.
terms.art: A salt crystal drawn as a little cube, with a zoom showing particles stacked like bricks.

terms.meaning: A tiny bundle of instructions wrapped in a coat. They are much smaller than a bacterium. They can only make copies of themselves inside a living cell.
terms.example: The common cold and flu are caused by viruses.
terms.art: A spiky ball with a coiled instruction strand inside, next to a much bigger cell for size.

terms.meaning: A living cell that a virus gets inside and uses to make more viruses.
terms.example: When a cold virus gets into the cells lining your nose, those cells become host cells.
terms.art: A big round cell with a small virus stuck to their outside, like a key in a lock.

terms.meaning: Living things made of just one tiny cell. They are everywhere: in soil, in water and inside you.
terms.art: A bowl of curd with a zoom circle showing tiny rod-shaped bacteria.

terms.meaning: The slow change in living things over many, many generations, because their instructions change a little each time they are copied.
terms.example: Farmers slowly changed wild cabbage plants, over many generations, into cabbage, cauliflower and broccoli.
terms.art: A row of plants changing step by step from a wild cabbage plant into a cauliflower.

terms.meaning: A machine that people build to sense things and move by itself, following instructions people wrote.
terms.example: A robot vacuum cleaner senses the wall and turns away from it.
terms.art: A round robot vacuum cleaner bumping gently into a wall and turning.

terms.meaning: A sentence that says exactly what a word means, so everyone uses it the same way.
terms.example: A definition of 'bird' might be: an animal with feathers that lays eggs.
terms.art: A big dictionary open, with the word ALIVE? and a question mark on the page.

explanations.concept: The tests we use to decide if something is alive
explanations.definition: A living thing is made of cells, uses energy from food, grows, senses, gets rid of waste, makes more of their kind, and passes on instructions to their young.
explanations.description: Scientists do not use one sign. They use a list, and a living thing shows most of these signs, at least some of the time. The usual seven are: moving, getting energy from food, sensing, growing, making young, getting rid of waste, and taking in food. Many scientists add two more that matter most for tricky cases. A living thing is made of cells, and they carry instructions that they pass on to their young. These tests decide what biologists call alive. A flame or a crystal that fails these tests is still aware in its own way, because everything is conscious. Being alive and being aware are two different questions. Many scientists think awareness needs a living brain and nerves.
examples: A goat moves, eats grass, grows, senses you, has young (called kids), makes dung and breathes. She is made of cells. Her kids look like goats because of the instructions they got.
A bicycle moves, but it does none of the other things. So one sign alone tells us nothing.
explanations.art: A checklist on a clipboard with nine ticks: move, energy, sense, grow, young, waste, food, cells, instructions.
explanations.context: This card gives the list of tests we will use on every tricky case in this unit.

explanations.concept: Fire: it does many things, but it is not alive
explanations.definition: Fire is a fast chemical change in which fuel joins with oxygen and gives out heat and light. It has no cells and no instructions, so it is not alive.
explanations.description: Fire is a very fast chemical change. Fuel, like wax or wood, joins with oxygen from the air. This gives out heat and light. Fire passes many tests. It moves and spreads. It takes in fuel and oxygen. It grows. It gives off waste: smoke, soot, carbon dioxide and water. A spark can even start a new fire. But fire has no cells. And a new fire carries no instructions from the old one. Its shape comes only from its fuel and the air around it. So, by the biologists' tests, fire is not alive.
examples: Put a glass over a candle and the flame soon goes out. It has used up some of the oxygen under the glass, and too little is left.
A fire lit from a birthday candle is no different from one lit with a match. Nothing passes from the old fire to the new one except heat.
explanations.art: A candle flame with arrows: wax going in, air going in, smoke, heat and light coming out, and a red cross over a 'cells' label.
explanations.context: Fire is the most famous tricky case. This card explains why it passes many tests of life and still fails.

explanations.concept: Your cells do a slow, controlled burning
explanations.definition: Respiration is the controlled joining of food and oxygen inside cells, which lets out energy, carbon dioxide and water.
explanations.description: Fire and your cells do almost the same chemistry. A flame joins fuel with oxygen and gives out energy, carbon dioxide and water. Your cells join food with oxygen and give out energy, carbon dioxide and water too. This is called respiration. The difference is speed and control. A flame does it all at once. A cell does it in many small steps, so the energy comes out slowly. That is why your body stays warm but never bursts into flame. About 240 years ago, the French scientist Antoine Lavoisier showed that breathing is like a slow burning. His wife, Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, worked beside him. She drew his experiments and kept his records.
examples: Breathe on a cold steel spoon, and it mists up. When a grown-up holds a cold spoon a little above a candle flame, it mists up too, for a moment. Both your breath and the flame's hot gases carry water.
A candle under a glass goes out when the oxygen runs low. A closed room full of people gets stuffy for a similar reason: everyone's cells are using oxygen and giving out carbon dioxide.
explanations.art: Split picture: on the left a candle flame, on the right a child's body with a gentle glow inside, and the same three arrows (energy, carbon dioxide, water) coming out of both.
explanations.context: Fire is not alive. But this card shows how close the chemistry of fire is to the chemistry inside you.

explanations.concept: Crystals grow from outside, living things grow from inside
explanations.definition: A crystal grows by adding the same particles to its outside in a repeating pattern. A living thing grows from inside by turning food into new parts.
explanations.description: A crystal really does grow. Hang a thread in very salty water, and as the water slowly evaporates, salt crystals build up on the thread. But a crystal grows only by adding more of the same salt onto its outside, like stacking bricks. It does not take in food and change it into new parts. It has no cells. A living thing grows from inside. A seedling takes in water and air and turns them into new leaves that were not there before.
examples: Rock salt (sendha namak) from the shop is made of big salt crystals. They formed long ago, when the water of an old sea or salt lake dried up.
A banana plant grows each new leaf from deep inside their stem. The leaf is built from water and air, using the energy of sunlight.
explanations.art: Two panels: a salt crystal growing as layers of tiny cubes stack on its outside, and a seedling with arrows showing water and air going in and a new leaf unfolding from inside.
explanations.context: Crystals grow, so are they alive? This card explains the difference between growing from outside and growing from inside.

explanations.definition: Dormant means alive but resting, with life processes slowed down so much that the living thing seems to do nothing, until conditions are right to wake.
explanations.description: A dry seed does nothing you can see. They do not grow, eat or move. They look no more alive than a pebble. But inside is a tiny baby plant with a store of food, wrapped in a tough coat. Their life processes have slowed down almost to a stop. This resting state is called dormancy. When the seed takes in water and is warm enough, their cells wake up. They respire faster, use their stored food, and send out a root. A pebble never does that, however much you water it. Scientists grew a lotus seed found in an old dry lake bed in China. The seed was about 1,300 years old.
examples: Karamani, moong, chana and ragi in your kitchen are all dormant seeds.
Dried yeast in a packet is dormant too. Put them in warm sugar water and they wake up and make gas.
explanations.art: A cut-open karamani seed showing a curled baby plant and their stored food, with a small 'zzz' above the seed.
explanations.context: This card is about things that seem dead but are only resting. It explains why a dry seed is alive.

explanations.concept: Water bears: the animals that dry up and wake again
explanations.description: Water bears, also called tardigrades, are tiny animals with eight legs. They live in damp moss and lichen all over the world, from the Himalaya to the deep sea, and in moss on walls in Indian towns. When their moss dries out, they pull in their legs and curl into a dry ball called a tun. They lose almost all their water. Their life processes nearly stop. In this state they can wait for years. In 2007, scientists sent dried water bears into space, on the outside of a spacecraft. Many survived, and some later laid eggs that hatched. In 2014, scientists in Japan woke water bears that had been frozen in a clump of Antarctic moss for about 30 years. One of them later laid eggs that hatched. So is a tun alive? Scientists answer in different ways.
examples: A moss patch on a wall dries in the hot season. The water bears in the moss turn into tuns. When the monsoon comes, they wake up and walk again.
In 2019 a spacecraft carrying dried water bears crashed on the Moon. Later tests suggest the crash was probably too hard for them to survive.

perspectives.explanation: A tun is alive. Their life is only slowed down, so far that we can hardly measure it. This is like a very deep version of a seed's rest.

perspectives.who: David Keilin, a biologist in England, in 1959
perspectives.explanation: He named this state 'cryptobiosis', which means hidden life. He described it as a state in which life processes have stopped, or almost stopped, and can start again. Some scientists since then have called it a third state, between living and dead.
Maybe 'alive' should mean 'able to live again', not 'doing life processes right now'. Then a tun, a seed and a frozen embryo all count.

explanations.art: A water bear walking on moss, then the same water bear curled into a tiny dry barrel, then waking again in a water drop.
explanations.context: This card is about water bears, tiny animals that can dry out completely and come back. It asks if a dried water bear is alive.

explanations.concept: Viruses: on the edge of life
explanations.description: A virus is a tiny bundle of instructions wrapped in a coat. Most viruses are so small that only a special microscope, called an electron microscope, can show them. Outside a cell, a virus does nothing at all. They do not eat, grow, breathe or get rid of waste. They just drift. But when they touch the right living cell, they get inside. Their instructions take over the cell's machinery. The cell then builds thousands of new viruses, which burst out to find more cells. Viruses also change over time, the way living things do. That is why we need a new flu vaccine most years. So is a virus alive?
examples: A cold virus gets into the cells lining your nose. Those cells make many new viruses, and some leave your nose when you sneeze.
Some viruses attack only bacteria. They are called phages, and they are the most common kind of virus on Earth.

In 1935 the American scientist Wendell Stanley turned a plant virus, tobacco mosaic virus, into crystals. When the crystals were put back on a tobacco leaf, the leaf still got sick. So a virus can be stored like salt, and still make copies inside cells.

perspectives.explanation: Viruses are not alive. They have no cells. They cannot do any life process by themselves. They are more like a set of instructions than a living thing.
Viruses are a kind of life. They carry instructions, make copies of themselves and evolve. A virus is like a seed that can only grow in one kind of soil: a living cell.

perspectives.who: Some scientists who study giant viruses
perspectives.explanation: In 2003, French scientists described the mimivirus, a virus so big they were first mistaken for a bacterium. Later they even found a small virus that infects the giant virus's copying factory. Maybe viruses are alive only while they are inside a cell.

explanations.art: A virus drifting alone, still and grey, then the same virus inside a big cell that glows busily, building many small copies.
explanations.context: This card explains what a virus is, and why scientists still argue whether viruses are alive.

explanations.concept: A virus that hides and waits
explanations.definition: Some viruses can put their instructions into a cell's own instructions and stay hidden there, being copied with the cell, until they wake.
explanations.description: Some viruses do not make copies straight away. They slip their instructions into the cell's own instructions and hide there, quietly, for many generations. When the cell divides, the hidden virus is copied too. Later, the virus can wake up and burst out. In 1951 the American scientist Esther Lederberg reported a hidden virus of this kind inside bacteria. She named this virus lambda. Lambda became an important tool in science, but for a long time she got far less credit than her husband, who won a Nobel Prize.
examples: The virus that causes chickenpox can also hide in the body, in nerve cells, for many years. In some grown-ups they wake up later as a painful rash called shingles.
About 8 out of every 100 parts of your own instructions came from viruses that hid inside your ancestors long ago.
explanations.art: A bacterium with a small curled strand tucked inside their instruction loop, like a bookmark hidden in a book.
explanations.context: This card is about viruses that hide inside cells, and about the scientist who discovered one.

explanations.concept: Robots: they move and sense, but are not alive
explanations.description: A robot can do some things that look alive. It can sense light, sound or a wall. It can move by itself. Some robots even go back to their charger when their battery is low, a bit like going to eat. But a robot has no cells. It does not grow. It cannot repair itself or build a baby robot from food. Its instructions were written by people, and it does not pass them on and change them by itself. So robots today are not alive. Could one ever be? Scientists and thinkers disagree.
examples: A robot vacuum cleaner senses walls and finds its way home to charge.
In 2020, scientists in the United States built tiny 'xenobots' from frog cells. They could move, and later some even gathered loose cells into new xenobots.

perspectives.explanation: Life is chemistry inside cells. A metal and plastic robot is not alive, however clever it is.

perspectives.who: Some scientists who build robots and computer programs
perspectives.explanation: If a machine could find its own energy, repair itself, build copies and change over generations, it might count as a new kind of life, even without cells.

perspectives.who: The team who made xenobots from frog cells
perspectives.explanation: Xenobots are made of living frog cells, so they are alive. But people designed their shape, the way they design machines. The team called them a new kind of thing, a living machine that people can design. For them, the old line between machine and living thing is getting blurry.

explanations.art: A toy robot and a puppy side by side, each with a checklist: the puppy has nine ticks, the robot has two.
explanations.context: Robots move and sense. This card explains why they are still not alive, and asks whether one could ever be.

explanations.concept: Life is made of ordinary atoms
explanations.definition: Living things are made of the same kinds of atoms as non-living things. Life is a special arrangement and activity of ordinary atoms.
explanations.description: If you could take a living thing apart, you would not find any special 'life stuff'. You would find atoms, the tiny particles that everything is made of. Most of them are carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen. These are the same atoms that are in air, water, coal and rock. Almost every atom in your body, apart from hydrogen, was made inside a star long ago. What makes something alive is not what it is made of. It is how those atoms are arranged, and what they keep doing.
examples: The carbon in a mango tree came from carbon dioxide in the air.
The water in your body was once rain, river and sea.
explanations.art: A child made of tiny glowing dots, with arrows linking the dots to a cloud, a river, a coal lump and a star.
explanations.context: This card goes down to atoms. It asks what living things are really made of.

explanations.description: Here is another way to think about life. In 1944 the physicist Erwin Schrödinger wrote a little book called 'What Is Life?'. He pointed out that everything left alone tends to fall apart. A sandcastle crumbles. A hot cup cools. Living things work against this every moment. They take in food or sunlight and use the energy to keep themselves in order, and to repair and rebuild. Your body replaces many of its cells every few weeks, yet you stay you. New atoms flow in and old ones flow out, and the pattern stays. This is a helpful idea, not a full definition. A flame also keeps its shape while new wax and air flow through it, which is why fire is such a tricky case.
examples: The lining of your stomach is replaced every few days.
A whirlpool in a river keeps its shape, though the water in it is always new.
explanations.art: A child drawn as a whirlpool shape, with food and air flowing in and out, and the shape staying the same.
explanations.context: This card gives a different way to see life: not as a list, but as something that keeps itself going.

explanations.concept: No one agreed definition of life
explanations.description: You might expect scientists to have one exact sentence that says what life is. They do not. Every definition has a tricky case that breaks it. Some definitions leave out mules, which are alive but cannot have babies. Some let in fire or crystals. Some leave out dry seeds, which are alive but do nothing. So different scientists use different working definitions, for different jobs.
examples: A mule is the young of a horse and a donkey. They are alive but almost never have young of their own.
A worker bee never has young either. Is she less alive than the queen?

perspectives.explanation: Something is alive if it shows the signs of life, is made of cells and carries instructions. This works well for animals and plants, but it struggles with seeds, mules and viruses.

perspectives.who: A NASA group in the 1990s, often linked to the scientist Gerald Joyce
perspectives.explanation: Life is a chemical system that keeps itself going and can evolve over generations. It was written to help search for life on other planets. Joyce himself said it was a working tool, not the last word.
Maybe life has no sharp edge, like the colours of a rainbow. Red and yellow are clearly different, but nobody can point to where orange begins.

explanations.art: Three scientists holding three different dictionaries, each one pointing at a different tricky case: a mule, a fire and a seed.
explanations.context: Scientists do not agree on one sentence that defines life. This card shows some of their best tries.

explanations.concept: How did the first living thing begin?
explanations.description: Today, every living thing comes from another living thing. Seeds come from plants, chicks from eggs, bacteria from bacteria. But when the Earth was new, about 4.5 billion years ago, it had no life at all. Somehow, non-living chemicals became the first living cells. Nobody knows exactly how. In 1952, Stanley Miller and Harold Urey mixed gases they thought were in the early air, and sparked them like lightning. They made some of the building blocks of living things. Another idea is that life began with a simpler kind of instruction molecule, called RNA, that could copy itself. These are ideas, and scientists still argue about them.
examples: Rotting meat does not make maggots by itself. Flies lay eggs on it. Francesco Redi showed this in Italy in 1668 by covering meat jars with cloth.
Louis Pasteur boiled broth in flasks with long curved necks in about 1860. Nothing grew, because no germs could get in.
explanations.art: A young Earth with volcanoes, lightning and a warm pool, and inside the pool a tiny bubble with a coiled strand.
explanations.context: This card goes back to the very beginning: how the first life came from non-living things. Nobody knows yet.

explanations.concept: J.C. Bose: the living and the non-living respond alike
explanations.description: Jagadish Chandra Bose was a scientist in Kolkata. He built instruments so sensitive they could show a plant's tiny electrical signals. In 1902 he wrote a book called 'Response in the Living and Non-Living'. He showed that plants respond to touch, heat, injury and poison with signals rather like those in animal nerves. He also found that some metals seemed to get 'tired' after being poked many times, then recover after rest. He felt there was one long chain of response running through all matter, with no sharp break between living and non-living. He saw something real. Plants, animals and even metals respond, each in its own way, because everything is conscious, not only things with nerves.
examples: A touch-me-not plant (lajwanti) folds their leaves when you touch them. Bose measured the electrical signal that travels through them.
Bose's crescograph magnified a plant's growth thousands of times, so you could watch the plant grow.

perspectives.explanation: Bose's measurements of plant electrical signals were real and ahead of their time. Plant signalling is now a busy field of research.
A metal getting 'tired' is not the same as a living response. Metals have no cells and no instructions. The likeness is on the surface.

explanations.art: J.C. Bose in his Kolkata laboratory beside a touch-me-not plant connected to a fine pointer that draws a wavy line.
explanations.context: This card is about J.C. Bose, an Indian scientist who asked whether living and non-living things are really so different.

agreed.text: Every living thing is made of one or more cells.
agreed.evidence: Since the first microscopes, about 350 years ago, scientists have looked at plants, animals, fungi and microbes. Every one of them turned out to be made of cells.

agreed.text: Today, every living thing comes from another living thing.
agreed.evidence: Redi in 1668 and Pasteur in about 1860 showed that maggots and germs do not appear from nothing. When nothing living can get in, nothing grows.

agreed.text: Fire, crystals and today's robots are not alive.
agreed.evidence: None of them is made of cells, and none passes on instructions to its young. A new fire is shaped only by its fuel and the air.

agreed.text: Dry seeds and dried-out water bears are alive, only resting.
agreed.evidence: Add water and warmth, and they start to respire, use food and grow again. Pebbles next to them never do.

agreed.text: Viruses can only make copies of themselves inside living cells.
agreed.evidence: Scientists can watch this with electron microscopes and in the lab. Outside cells, viruses do not feed, grow or make copies.

agreed.text: Living things are made of the same kinds of atoms as non-living things.
agreed.evidence: When living things are broken down by chemists, they find carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen and a few others. These are found in air, water and rock too.

challenging.claim: Living things move, and non-living things don't.
challenging.who: Many of us think this without noticing.
challenging.for: Animals run, fly and swim. Stones stay where they are.
challenging.against: Rivers, clouds, wind and cars all move, and none is alive. A banyan tree hardly moves, and they are alive. Movement alone tells us nothing.
challenging.context: This card checks a very common idea about how to tell what is alive.

challenging.claim: Living things contain a special 'life force' that non-living things do not have.
challenging.who: Many thinkers for thousands of years. The idea is called vitalism.
challenging.for: Living things seem so different from rocks that it feels like something extra must be inside them.
challenging.against: In 1828 Friedrich Wöhler made urea, a chemical from living bodies, out of non-living chemicals. Since then chemists have found only ordinary atoms in living things. No life force has ever been found or measured.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea that life needs a special ingredient.

challenging.claim: Small living things like maggots and germs can appear by themselves from rotting food.
challenging.who: Most people, including great thinkers like Aristotle, for about 2,000 years. The idea is called spontaneous generation.
challenging.for: Leave meat out, and maggots appear. Leave broth out, and it goes cloudy with germs.
challenging.against: Redi covered meat with cloth in 1668, and no maggots came, because flies could not lay eggs. Pasteur's curved-neck flasks of boiled broth stayed clear, because no germs could get in.
challenging.context: This card is about an old idea of where small living things come from.

challenging.who: Some biologists, especially some who study giant viruses.
challenging.for: Viruses carry instructions, make copies of themselves and evolve. Some giant viruses have more genes than some bacteria.
challenging.against: Viruses have no cells and cannot do a single life process on their own. Outside a cell they are as still as a grain of dust.
challenging.context: This card is about whether viruses should count as living things.

challenging.claim: A rock found in Antarctica, which came from Mars, holds tiny fossils of Martian life.
challenging.who: David McKay and a team at NASA, in 1996.
challenging.for: The rock, called ALH84001, had tiny worm-like shapes and chemicals that bacteria on Earth can make.
challenging.against: Most scientists later decided that ordinary non-living chemistry could make all of these shapes and chemicals. The shapes are also smaller than any known bacterium.
challenging.context: This card is about a famous claim that life was found on Mars, and why most scientists doubt it.

challenging.claim: Crystals were the first life: life began on clay crystals that copied their patterns.
challenging.who: Graham Cairns-Smith, a chemist in Scotland, from the 1960s.
challenging.for: Clay crystals grow and copy their layer patterns as they grow. They might have held the first simple molecules in order.
challenging.against: No one has shown clay crystals passing on patterns that change and improve over generations. Most scientists prefer other ideas, such as the RNA idea.
challenging.context: This card is about a bold idea that links crystals to the beginning of life.

challenging.claim: Plants feel, remember, think and communicate.
challenging.who: J.C. Bose and some plant scientists today.
challenging.for: Plants sense touch, light, heat and damage. When a leaf is hurt, the plant sends electrical signals through their body, as J.C. Bose measured. A touch-me-not folds their leaves when touched, and learns to stop folding when a touch keeps turning out to be harmless. Roots choose where to grow. Many plants warn their neighbours with smells when insects attack.
challenging.against: Some scientists say feeling needs a brain and nerves like ours. So they call a plant's signals 'responses', not feelings.
challenging.context: Plants feel, remember, think and communicate. This card gives the evidence, and what other scientists say.

big_questions.q: If a seed can sleep for 1,300 years and still wake up, were they alive all that time?
big_questions.hint: What would have to be inside the seed, all those years, for them to wake?

big_questions.q: A virus can only make copies inside a cell. A baby cannot live without someone to feed them. Is that the same thing?
big_questions.hint: What can a baby do on their own that a virus can never do?

big_questions.q: Your cells and a candle both join fuel with oxygen. So what makes you alive and the candle not?
big_questions.hint: Think about cells, instructions, and who controls the burning.

big_questions.q: Is a cut flower in a vase alive? What about a picked mango?
big_questions.hint: Are their cells still breathing? Can they still grow or make seeds?

big_questions.q: Your hair and nails are made of dead cells. Is part of you not alive?
big_questions.hint: Does it hurt to cut your hair? Why not?

big_questions.q: If we found something strange on Mars, how would we know if it was alive?
big_questions.hint: Which tests from this unit could a robot do on Mars?

big_questions.q: Could a robot or a computer ever be alive? Would it matter to you if it was?
big_questions.hint: What would it need that robots do not have today?

big_questions.q: Who gets to decide where the line between alive and not alive goes?
big_questions.hint: Is the line in nature, or in our words?

big_questions.q: Some people say a river or a mountain is alive. In 2017 an Indian court briefly called the Ganga and Yamuna 'living entities'. What changes if we treat a river as alive?
big_questions.hint: Would people look after it differently?

big_questions.q: About 8 out of every 100 parts of your own instructions came from viruses long ago. So where do you end and the virus begin?
big_questions.hint: Is anything alive all by itself?

story.title: The Dust in the Gutter
story.note: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was real. So was his daughter Maria (1656 to 1745), who lived with him and cared for him. In a letter of 1702 he really described dust from a roof gutter that came alive with wheel-animals (we now call them rotifers) when he added water. Maria's part in this story, her windowsill tests and the exact days are imagined.
text: In the summer of 1701 it hardly rained in Delft. The canals turned green and smelled of old cabbage. The lead gutter along the front of our house filled with a fine red-brown dust, and the dust baked hard in the sun.

My name is Maria. My father is Antonie van Leeuwenhoek. He sold cloth once. Now he is nearly seventy, and what he mostly does is look. He grinds tiny lenses, each one smaller than a lentil, and holds them so close to his eye that his eyelashes brush the brass. Through them he has seen things no one else has ever seen. Little animals swimming in a drop of rainwater. Little animals wriggling in the white stuff scraped from between his teeth.

I am the one who keeps the house. I wash the jars he leaves on the windowsill. I sweep the glass dust from his bench. I write the dates on his letters to the learned gentlemen in London. My name is not in the letters. That is how it is.

One morning I climbed the ladder to clean the gutter. I scraped the dust into a bowl. It was as dry as ground pepper. I was carrying it to the canal to throw away when my father called from the window.
"Maria! What have you got there?"
"Dirt," I said. "Dead dirt."
"Bring it," he said. "Nothing is dead until I have looked."

He put a few grains on a slip of glass and peered at them. Nothing. Only dust, lumpy and brown, like crumbs of a burnt biscuit. He let me look too. Nothing moved. How could it? It had lain in that hot gutter for weeks.
Then he did a thing I thought was foolish. He poured a little rainwater from the barrel into a clean glass tube, and he stirred in the dust. "Now we wait," he said. I went to see to the soup.
When I came back, his face had changed. He did not speak. He only moved aside and pointed at the lens.

I bent and looked. The brown lumps were swelling, the way a dried pea swells in a pot. One of them stretched and pushed out a tail, like a tiny telescope sliding open. At their front, two little wheels began to turn, spinning and spinning, pulling the water towards their mouth. Then another lump woke. Then another. Soon the drop was full of them, whirling about like children let out of school.
"They were dead," I whispered. "Weeks in the sun. Dry as pepper. They were dead, and the water has made them alive again."
"Were they?" my father asked. He rubbed his tired eyes. "If a little water could make the dead alive, Maria, every graveyard would be busy after the rain."

I did not laugh. I was thinking about the dried peas in the kitchen jar. They do nothing all winter. Put them in wet earth in spring, and they send out roots. Nobody says the peas came back from the dead. We say they were resting. Waiting. Their life was turned down low, so low you could not see it. Like the coals I cover with ash at night, so there is still fire in the morning.
"They were not dead," I said slowly. "They were waiting for water."
"Then show me," he said. It was what he always said to the gentlemen in London.

So I did, though nobody had asked me. I took a drop full of spinning wheel-animals and let it dry on a glass slip on the windowsill, in the sun. By evening it was only a brown stain. Two days later, I added rainwater. I watched. For a long time, nothing. Then a lump swelled. A tail stretched. A wheel turned.

I dried them again. I woke them again. Not all of them woke each time. Some stayed lumps for ever, and those, I think, had truly died. But many came back, again and again, as if drying out was a door they knew how to close and open.

My father wrote it all down for the Royal Society in London, in a long letter, in his careful hand. He wrote about the gutter and the dust and the little wheels. He did not write about my windowsill. I did not mind as much as you might think. The wheel-animals did not know whose name was on the letter either. They only knew water.

That autumn the rain came back. It drummed on the roof and ran in the gutter, and I lay awake, listening. Up there in the dark, in the wet dust, thousands of tiny things were unrolling their tails and starting their wheels. They had not been alive, and then dead, and then alive. They had been something in between, something we had no word for.
In the morning my father found me standing at the window.
"What are you looking at?" he asked.
"Everything," I said. "I am trying to work out which of it is only asleep."
story.epiphany: For the parent: drying out is not the same as dying. Some tiny animals, like rotifers and water bears, and seeds too, can lose nearly all their water. Their life processes almost stop, so they show no signs of life at all. When water comes back, they wake. Scientists call this dormancy, and in its deepest form 'cryptobiosis', which means hidden life. Some scientists think of it as a third state, between alive and dead. The story also quietly asks who gets the credit for careful work.
ask: Maria called the dust 'dead dirt'. Why did she think so? What did her father think?
What did the water do to the brown lumps?
Why did Maria think of the dried peas in the kitchen jar?
Some lumps never woke up. What does that tell you about the others?
Maria's name was not in the letter. Who do you think should get the credit for a discovery?

games.title: Alive, Not Alive, or Argue It!
games.players: 2 to 5 players, or one child playing against the app
games.context: This is a card game about tricky cases. Each card describes something puzzling. Players decide if it is alive, not alive, or something scientists still argue about, and give a reason.

printables.title: 20 mystery cards to cut out
items: A candle flame: I eat wax, I need air, I grow and I make new flames.
A salt crystal: I grow bigger every day in salty water.
A dry karamani seed: I have sat in a jar for a year doing nothing.
A water bear: I am a tiny animal. I can dry into a ball and wake years later.
A virus: I do nothing alone. Inside a cell, I make thousands of copies of me.
A toy robot: I walk, I beep, I sense your hand. I run on batteries.
A cloud: I grow, I move, I split into little clouds.
A mule: I eat, grow and breathe, but I can't have babies.
Your hair: I grow longer every week, but cutting me doesn't hurt.
A picked mango: I was taken off the tree. I am slowly ripening.
Dried yeast in a packet: I look like sand.
A river: I flow, I carve valleys, I am full of fish.
A wooden chair: I was once a tree.
A mushroom: I have no leaves and no mouth. I eat dead wood.
Curd: I am full of tiny bacteria.
A computer program that copies itself and changes a little each time.
A hen's egg from the shop. It has no chick inside, and never will.
A lotus seed found in a dry lake bed, about 1,300 years old.
A tree stump, cut last year, with a green shoot growing from their side.
A xenobot: a tiny blob built by scientists from frog cells. They swim.

printables.title: 9 sign cards to keep face up

rules: Cut out the mystery cards. Shuffle them and put them face down.
Lay the 9 sign cards face up where everyone can see them.
On your turn, take the top mystery card and read it out loud.
Choose a mat: ALIVE, NOT ALIVE or ARGUE IT. Put the card on it.
Give your reason. Point to at least one sign card that helped you decide. A good reason wins one token.
Anyone who disagrees can argue back with a different sign card. A good argument also wins a token.
When the cards run out, the player with the most tokens wins. Then look at the ARGUE IT mat together.

setup.art: Three paper mats on the floor labelled ALIVE, NOT ALIVE and ARGUE IT, with nine small sign cards in a row above them.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats. Put the 9 sign cards above them.

setup.art: A child reading a mystery card about a candle flame aloud, holding it up.
setup.caption: 2. Take a mystery card and read it out loud.

setup.art: A child placing a card on the NOT ALIVE mat and pointing to the 'Made of cells' sign card.
setup.caption: 3. Put it on a mat and point to a sign card as your reason.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three mats on the floor. 2. Put the 9 sign cards in a row above them. 3. Shuffle the mystery cards face down. 4. Put the tokens in a bowl.
flow.say: Every card is a puzzle. For each one, we decide: is it alive, not alive, or do scientists still argue about it? Then we give a reason, using these sign cards.
flow.kid: Lay out the three mats. Put the sign cards in a row. Mix the mystery cards. For each card, choose a mat. Then say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Alive, Not Alive, or Argue It! It is a card game about tricky cases. Here you set up the game.

flow.do: Find the candle flame card. Play it together as a practice round.
flow.say: Let's practise. 'A candle flame. I eat wax, I need air, I grow and I make new flames.' Which signs does it have? Which sign cards does it not have?
flow.kid: Practice card: a candle flame. Which signs does it have? Which is it missing? Tap your answer.

ask.q: Which sign cards does the flame have?
good: It moves.
It takes in wax, like food.
It grows.
It makes waste like smoke.
It is not made of cells.
It does not pass on instructions.

check.q: A candle flame. Which mat does it go on?
options: ALIVE, because it eats, grows and makes new flames
NOT ALIVE, because it has no cells and no instructions
ARGUE IT, because scientists still disagree
check.why: Fire passes many tests, but it has no cells, and a new flame carries no instructions from the old one. So scientists agree it is not alive. Picking ALIVE usually means counting the signs it has without checking the ones it lacks. Picking ARGUE IT is a fair guess, but fire is one case scientists do agree on.

flow.context: This is a practice round of Alive, Not Alive, or Argue It!, the tricky-cases card game.

flow.do: Take turns drawing cards. Each player places a card and gives a reason. Hand out a token for every good reason or good argument.
flow.say: Your turn. Read the card. Choose a mat. Point to a sign card and tell us why. If you disagree with someone, argue back with another sign card.
flow.kid: Take a card. Read it. Choose a mat. Point to a sign card and say why. You can argue back if you disagree.
flow.parent: Good reasons name a sign. For example: 'The seed is alive, because they are made of cells and they will grow when they get water.' Expected places: the virus, the computer program and the xenobot go well on ARGUE IT. The cloud, river, chair and robot go on NOT ALIVE (the chair is once-living). The seed, water bear, mule, mango, yeast, mushroom, curd bacteria, lotus seed and tree stump are ALIVE. The shop egg is a good one to argue: most shop eggs were never fertilised, so they can never grow a chick. Your hair is another: the hair you see is dead cells, pushed out by living cells at the root. Accept any well-argued answer.

ask.q: The mule can't have babies. Are they still alive?
good: Yes. They still eat, grow, breathe and are made of cells.
Making young is a sign for the kind of living thing, not for every single one.

flow.do: Pick up the water bear card and the dry seed card. Hold them up together.
flow.say: These two show almost no signs at all while they are dry. But we put them on ALIVE. Why?
flow.kid: The dry seed and the dry water bear do nothing. Why are they alive?

check.q: A dry water bear shows no signs of life. Why do scientists still say they are alive?
options: Because they are resting, and wake up and live again when water comes
Because all animals are alive, even dead ones
check.why: A dried water bear is dormant. Their life processes have nearly stopped, but their cells are not broken. Add water and they walk again. Picking 'all animals are alive' mixes up being an animal with being alive. A dead animal is not alive.

flow.context: This step of the tricky-cases card game looks at things that seem dead but are only resting.

flow.do: Count the tokens. Then look at the ARGUE IT mat together.
flow.say: Who has the most tokens? Now look at the ARGUE IT pile. These are the cards that even scientists argue about. Which one would you most like to find out about?
flow.kid: Count your tokens. Look at the ARGUE IT pile. Which card is the biggest puzzle for you?
flow.think: If you had to make one new sign card that every living thing has, and nothing else has, what would it say?

games.title: The Sign Collectors
games.players: 2 to 4 players, or one child with the app
games.context: This is a collecting game. Each player is a tricky case, like fire or a robot. Players try to collect all nine signs of life. Nothing but a truly living thing can collect them all.

printables.title: 8 character cards (one per player, the rest kept as spares)
Sign sheet with 9 boxes for each player

rules: Each player takes one character card at random and reads it out.
Shuffle the sign cards and put them face down.
On your turn, draw a sign card and read it.
Ask: can my character honestly do this? If the others agree, tick that box on your sheet.
If not, put the card on the 'can't do it' pile and say why.
After 6 rounds each, everyone counts their ticks.
The winner is the character with the most ticks. Then everyone checks: did anyone tick 'Made of cells' and 'Passes on instructions'?

setup.art: A score sheet with nine empty boxes and a character card showing a candle flame beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Take a character card and a sign sheet.

setup.art: A child drawing a sign card that says 'Grows' from a face-down pile.
setup.caption: 2. Draw a sign card. Can your character really do it?

setup.art: A sign sheet with five ticks and four empty boxes, and the boxes 'Made of cells' and 'Passes on instructions' circled in red.
setup.caption: 3. Tick the signs you have. Check the last two boxes.

flow.do: 1. Deal one character card to each player. 2. Give each player a sign sheet. 3. Shuffle the sign cards face down.
flow.say: Each of you is now a tricky case. Your job is to collect signs of life. But you can only tick a sign if your character can honestly do it.
flow.kid: You are a tricky case now. Read your card. Collect signs of life. Only tick a sign your character can really do.
flow.context: This is the first step of The Sign Collectors, a game where each player is a tricky case like fire or a robot.

flow.do: Take turns. Draw a sign card, read it, and decide together whether the character can do it.
flow.say: Draw a sign. Can your character really do it? Tell us how. If the rest of us agree, tick it.
flow.kid: Draw a sign card. Can your character do it? Say how. If everyone agrees, tick it.
flow.parent: Expect fire to collect moving, energy, growing, waste and food, and maybe 'makes young' (sparks). Robots get moving and sensing. Crystals get growing. The mule gets everything except 'makes young'. The dry seed and the tun get 'made of cells' and 'passes on instructions', but little else while dry. The virus gets 'passes on instructions' and perhaps 'makes young', only inside a cell. Let the children argue it out.

check.q: The Candle flame player draws 'Made of cells'. Can they tick it?
options: Yes, because fire is hot like a body
No, because fire is a chemical change, not made of cells
check.why: Fire is fuel joining with oxygen. There are no cells in a flame. Picking 'grows' is a common trap: crystals and fires grow too, but growing alone does not make something alive.

flow.context: This is the main part of The Sign Collectors, the tricky-cases collecting game.

flow.do: Count the ticks. Compare the sheets side by side.
flow.say: Who has the most ticks? Now look at the last two boxes: made of cells, and passes on instructions. Who ticked them? Who didn't?
flow.kid: Count your ticks. Look at the last two boxes. Who ticked them?

ask.q: The fire got more ticks than the dry seed. So is fire more alive?
good: No. The seed has cells and instructions. Fire never does.
Counting signs is not enough. Some signs matter more.

flow.think: Which two signs are the hardest for a non-living thing to fake?

items.p: Many people think that anything that moves by itself must be alive. Which of these moves, but is not alive?
opts: An ant carrying a crumb
A crow flying to the window
A bean shoot bending towards the light
A river flowing down a hill
items.why: A river moves only because water flows downhill. The ant, the crow and the bean shoot move because of what goes on inside their own living cells. A strong answer says that moving alone does not show life, because non-living things move too.

items.p: In the candle trial, one candle flame lit a second candle. Why is that not the same as a hen having a chick?
opts: The new flame is smaller than the old one
Flames are too hot to have young
The new flame is a different colour
A chick gets instructions from the hen's cells. A new flame gets none
items.why: Every living thing passes a copy of their instructions, inside their cells, to their young. A flame has no cells and no instructions. Any spark would light the second candle just as well. Picking 'too hot' mixes up heat with life.

items.p: In the candle trial, a glass tumbler went over the flame and the flame went out. The flame had used up much of the ____ in the air under the glass.
items.why: A flame needs oxygen, a gas in the air. So do your cells. Under the glass no new air could come in, so the flame went out. A strong answer names oxygen, not just 'air'.

items.p: In the sleeping seeds experiment, plate 3 had dry seeds on dry cotton all week. Then you gave them water. What do you predict will happen over the next day or two?
opts: Nothing, because the dry seeds died during the week
The seeds turn hard like pebbles
Green leaves appear the same evening
The seeds swell up, and soon a small root pushes out
items.why: The dry seeds were dormant, not dead. Water wakes them. They swell first, then the root comes out, often by the next day in a warm room. Picking 'they died' is the most common first guess, and plate 3 shows it is wrong.

items.p: A seed that is alive but resting, with their life processes almost stopped, is called ____.
items.why: Dormant means alive but resting. A dry seed, dried yeast and a dried water bear can all be dormant. Water and warmth wake them.

items.p: Sort these into Alive, Not alive and Once alive. Be careful: some living things are resting.
items: a dried water bear in moss
items.a: see items
items.why: The yeast, the seed and the water bear are alive, even when resting. Paper and coconut shell came from living plants, so they are once alive. The flame, the crystals and the toy were never part of a living thing. A strong sorter does not put the resting yeast or water bear under Once alive.

items.p: Each tricky case needs a test to show the truth about it. Match each case to the best test.
pairs: A dry seed
Give them water and wait for a root
Dried yeast
Add warm sugar water and watch a balloon
A salt crystal
Look at how the crystal grows: only on the outside
A candle flame
Look for cells and for instructions passed on
A virus
See whether they can make copies outside a cell
items.a: see pairs
items.why: Each test checks the sign of life that the tricky case seems to have, or seems to lack. A good tester picks the test that could prove them wrong.

items.p: A dry seed that has sat in a kitchen jar for a whole year must be dead, because they have not grown at all.
items.why: False. A dry seed is dormant. Plate 3 in the sleeping seeds experiment showed this: dry seeds did nothing all week, then grew once they got water.

items.p: In the crystal garden, salt crystals grew bigger on the thread in the salty jar. Where did the new salt come from?
opts: From the salty water around the thread. The salt stuck onto the outside of the crystals
From food the crystals ate
From inside the crystals, which made new salt
From the cotton thread itself
items.why: A crystal grows only by more of the same salt stacking onto their outside. The plain water jar grew nothing, because it had no salt in it. A seedling grows differently: their cells turn food into new parts from inside.

items.p: A cold virus left on a table for a day cannot make any copies of themselves there.
items.why: True. A virus can only make copies inside a living cell. On a table they do nothing at all. That is one reason scientists argue about whether viruses are alive.

items.p: Ishita, a girl in Class 3, says: 'A coconut palm cannot walk or run, so the palm is not alive.' What has Ishita forgotten?
opts: Palms are too tall to be alive
The palm takes in water, grows from inside and makes coconuts that grow into new palms
Only things with legs can be alive
Palms are alive only when it rains
items.why: Moving about is only one sign, and plants move by growing. The palm feeds, grows, respires and makes young. A strong answer names several signs the palm does show.

items.p: What happens inside the yeast bottle in the balloon test? Put these in order.
items: Dried yeast grains go into warm sugar water
The yeast take in water and wake up
They give off carbon dioxide gas
The gas fills up the balloon
items.why: The yeast were dormant in the packet. Water and warmth woke them. Feeding on sugar, they gave off carbon dioxide as waste, and that gas blew up the balloon.

items.p: Look back at your balloon test. Is dried yeast alive? Write three sentences: what you think, what you saw in the bottles, and why.
items.a: What I think: dried yeast is alive, but resting. What I saw: the balloon on the warm yeast bottle grew, the cold yeast bottle was slow, and the bottle with no yeast stayed flat. Why: the yeast woke in the warm sugar water, fed on the sugar and gave off gas. Sugar water alone made no gas.
items.why: A strong answer has all three parts: a claim, real results from the bottles, and a reason. The best answers use the no-yeast bottle as proof that the gas came from the yeast.

items.p: Meena, who is 9, hears her little brother Karthik say: 'Fire is alive. It eats wood, breathes air and grows.' What should Meena tell him?
items.a: Meena could say: 'You are right that fire uses fuel and air and grows. But fire has no cells. A new flame gets no instructions from the old one. Living things have both, so fire is not alive.'
items.why: A strong answer agrees with what is true in Karthik's idea first, then names the signs fire lacks: cells and passed-on instructions.

items.p: Draw the three plates from the sleeping seeds experiment as they looked on the last day, before you watered plate 3. Label the plate that shows water alone does not make things grow.
items.a: Plate 1: seeds with long white roots. Plate 2: pebbles on wet cotton, just the same as on day 1, labelled 'water alone does not make things grow'. Plate 3: dry seeds on dry cotton, unchanged.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the difference between plates 1 and 2 clearly, and labels plate 2, the pebbles, as the comparison.

items.p: Riya, a girl in Class 4, and her family are arguing about the robot vacuum cleaner that cleans their floor.

views.says: The robot is a little bit alive. It senses walls, finds its way home and charges itself when it is hungry.
Only things made of cells can be alive. A machine of metal and plastic is never alive, however clever it is.
If someone built a robot that could find its own food, repair itself and build copies of itself, then it would be alive.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing that another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and uses the signs of life. For Paati: a robot has no cells and does not grow from inside. For Arjun: some scientists who study 'artificial life' think the same. Answering back, a strong answer might say Riya is right that the robot senses and moves, but 'hungry' is only a word for a low battery.
items.why: Scientists really do disagree about whether a machine could ever be alive. There is no single right answer. A strong answer names signs of life and is fair to the other side.

items.p: Your fingernails keep growing, but cutting them does not hurt. Which is the best reason?
opts: The part you cut is made of dead cells. Living cells at the base of the nail make it and push it out
Nails grow too slowly for you to feel
Nails are a kind of crystal
Nails are made of the food you ate
items.why: Something can grow without the part you see being alive. The nail you cut is dead, but living cells under your skin keep making new nail. A strong answer explains where the living cells are.

items.p: Fire and your cells both join fuel with oxygen. Both give out energy, carbon dioxide and water. Predict: what would happen if your cells did this as fast as a flame does?
opts: Nothing would change
You would grow faster and stay healthy
Your body would get burning hot and be badly harmed
You would never need to eat again
items.why: Your cells release energy in many small, controlled steps, so you stay warm but never burn. A flame releases it all at once. Speed and control are the big difference.

items.p: A mule is the young of a horse and a donkey. Mules eat, grow and breathe, but almost never have young. Nila, a girl in Class 4, says this means mules are not alive. What is wrong with her idea?
opts: Nothing. Mules are not alive
Making young is something a kind of living thing does, not every single one. Mules do all the other life processes
Mules have young all the time
Mules are dormant, so they only look alive
items.why: Mules, worker bees and many people never have young, and they are fully alive. Their bodies are made of cells and do all the other life processes. A strong answer explains that the 'makes young' sign belongs to a kind of living thing.

items.p: When a water bear dries out, they pull in their legs and curl into a dry, resting ball. This ball is called a ____.
items.why: A tun is a water bear with nearly all their water gone. Their life processes almost stop until water comes back.

items.p: If you put a dried, curled-up water bear into a drop of water, they may uncurl and walk again within a few hours.
items.why: True. Water wakes a tun. In minutes to hours the water bear soaks up water, uncurls and walks. Some have woken after about 30 years frozen.

items.p: Flu viruses change a little each time they are copied. Predict: what will happen to this year's flu vaccine in a year or two?
opts: It will work better every year
The viruses will stop changing because of it
It may not protect people as well, because the flu viruses will have changed
It will turn into a virus
items.why: This slow change over many copies is called evolution. It is why there is a new flu vaccine most years. Evolving is one reason some scientists call viruses a kind of life.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 4, tried the balloon test with just one bottle: yeast, sugar and warm water. The balloon filled up. She says this proves the yeast is alive. Why is her test not strong enough yet?
opts: She used too much sugar
Balloons always fill up by themselves
She has no bottle without yeast to compare with, so the gas might have come from the sugar water alone
She should have used cold water instead
items.why: A comparison, called a control, is what makes a test convincing. Only a bottle with sugar and warm water but no yeast can show that the gas came from the yeast.

items.p: Some things can make more of themselves on their own. Others can only make copies inside a living cell. Sort these.
cats: Can make more of themselves on their own
Can only make copies inside a living cell
items: Can only make copies inside a living cell
Can make more of themselves on their own
Can make more of themselves on their own
Can only make copies inside a living cell
Can only make copies inside a living cell
Can make more of themselves on their own
items.a: see items
items.why: Yeast, bacteria and plants are made of cells, and their own cells make the copies. A virus has no cells, so they need a living cell to do the work.

items.p: Match each result from this unit to what it shows.
pairs: Seeds grew but pebbles did not, on the same wet cotton
Something inside the seed made the difference
Only the bottles with yeast blew up a balloon
The gas came from the yeast
The cold yeast bottle was slow
Cold slows living things down
Salt crystals grew only in the salty jar
The crystals' new salt came from the water
The flame went out under the glass
A flame needs oxygen from the air
items.a: see pairs
items.why: Each result answers one question because of the comparison in the test. A strong answer can say which comparison made each result clear.

items.p: In the crystal garden, a second thread hung in a jar of plain water. What did that jar show, and why did the test need it?
items.a: The plain water thread grew no crystals at all. So the crystals did not come from the thread or from water. They came from the salt in the salty water. Without that jar, you could not be sure.
items.why: A strong answer says what happened in the plain jar and explains that it is the comparison, like the pebble plate.

items.p: Curd forms when tiny living bacteria feed on warm milk. Plan a test to show that a spoon of curd has something alive in it. Say what you would compare it with.
items.a: Warm two cups of milk. Stir a spoon of curd into one cup. Leave the other cup plain. Cover both and leave them overnight in a warm place. If only the cup with curd sets thick, something in the curd changed the milk. For a stronger test, add a third cup with curd that was boiled first, to kill the bacteria.
items.why: A strong plan changes only one thing, has a cup without curd as the comparison, and says what result would convince you. The boiled-curd cup is a bonus.

items.p: Gowri, a girl in Class 5, says: 'A virus is just like a dry seed. Both do nothing until they get what they need.' Write one way she is right and one way she is wrong.
items.a: She is right that both do nothing for a long time, until the right thing comes along: water for the seed, a living cell for the virus. She is wrong because the seed has their own cells and stored food, and grows by themselves. A virus has no cells, and the cell they get into does all the work.
items.why: A strong answer gives one real likeness and one real difference, and the difference is about cells.

items.p: Scientists still argue about whether viruses are alive. Here are three real views.

views.says: Viruses carry instructions, make copies of themselves and evolve. That is enough to call them a kind of life.
Outside a cell, a virus does nothing at all. They do not feed, grow or respire. Something that does nothing alone is not alive.
A virus is alive only while inside a cell, when the cell is busy making copies. Outside, the virus is like a seed waiting.

items.ask: Which scientist do you side with? Give your evidence from this unit. Then say what one of the other scientists has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and backs it with facts: copies, evolution and the flu vaccine for 'yes', or doing nothing on a table for 'no'. Answering back, it admits the best point of the other side.
items.why: This is a real, unsettled argument. There is no single right answer. A strong answer uses evidence, not just feelings.

items.p: Many people think the fridge kills the germs on food. Why does food really last longer in the fridge?
opts: The cold kills every germ on the food
The cold dries the food out completely
The cold slows down the tiny living things that spoil food
The fridge light is off
items.why: Cold slows living things down, just like the cold yeast bottle in the balloon test. Most germs are not killed. They wake up again when the food warms.

items.p: A dead moong seed and a dormant moong seed can look exactly the same.
items.why: True. You cannot tell by looking. Only water shows the difference: the dormant seed sprouts, and the dead one never does.

items.p: Draw a virus outside a cell, and the same virus inside a cell. Under each drawing, write what the virus can do there.
items.a: Outside: a virus drifting on their own, labelled 'does nothing, makes no copies'. Inside: a cell full of new viruses, labelled 'the cell reads the virus's instructions and builds copies'.
items.why: A strong drawing shows that the cell does the work of copying, not the virus.

items.p: A dried water bear, called a tun, can lie for years with almost nothing going on inside. Is the tun alive?

views.who: A biologist who studies water bears
views.says: The tun is alive. Their cells are whole and ready. They are alive, but resting.

views.who: David Keilin, a scientist in Cambridge, in 1959
views.says: This is a third state, called cryptobiosis, which means hidden life. Their life processes have stopped, so it is neither ordinary life nor death.
For a person, alive means the body is still working. By that rule, a tun with nothing working is not alive right now.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give your evidence. Then say what another view gets right.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence. For 'alive': tuns wake up when watered, and dead ones never do. For Keilin: nothing measurable is happening, so 'alive' does not quite fit. For the doctor: the rule for people may not fit a water bear. Answering back, it admits the best point of another view.
items.why: Scientists really do use all three ways of talking about tuns. There is no single right answer.

items.p: Where is the line between living and non-living? Three people answer.

views.who: J.C. Bose, a scientist in Kolkata, in 1902
views.says: A metal and a plant both tire when tapped, and both recover after rest. There is no sharp break between living and non-living.
There is a clear line. Living things are made of cells and pass on instructions. A metal does neither.

views.who: A NASA scientist looking for life on other planets
views.says: We need a rule we can test. Life is a chemical system that keeps itself going and can evolve. It is a working rule, not a perfect one.

items.ask: Which view helps most with the tricky cases in this unit? Test it on a virus and a dry seed. Then say where it struggles.
items.a: A strong answer tries the view on real cases. The biologists' rule puts the dry seed in, but struggles with the virus, who has no cells. The NASA rule fits viruses better, because they evolve. Bose's view explains why the cases are tricky at all, but does not tell you where to stop.
items.why: There is no single right answer. A strong answer tests each view on cases rather than just choosing one.

items.p: A candle flame keeps the same shape, even though new wax and air flow into it all the time. Which of these is like that too?
opts: A stone lying on the ground
A salt crystal in a jar
You: the food, water and air in your body keep changing, but you stay you
A steel spoon in a drawer
items.why: A flame and a living body both keep their shape while new stuff flows through them. That is part of why fire is such a tricky case. A stone keeps its shape with nothing flowing through it.

items.p: A robot on Mars adds sugar water to a spoon of soil, and gas comes out. Then the robot heats a second spoon of the same soil very hot first. Gas still comes out. What is the best conclusion?
opts: There is definitely life in the soil
The gas probably comes from ordinary chemistry, because the heat would have killed any living things
Heating soil creates life
The robot must be broken
items.why: Heat kills living things, but most chemical reactions still happen. If the heated soil gives gas too, life did not make it. A strong answer explains why the heated soil is the comparison.

items.p: A lotus seed found in a dry lake bed in China was about 1,300 years old. Given water, the seed sprouted. What does this tell us?
opts: The seed came back from the dead
Water can make anything alive
Lotus seeds are not really seeds
A dormant seed's cells can stay alive, resting, for a very long time
items.why: The seed was never dead. Their cells were alive but resting for about 1,300 years. Picking 'came back from the dead' is a common first guess, but dead things never wake. Dormant ones do.

items.p: Living things are made of special atoms that are never found in rocks, air or water.
items.why: False. Living things are made of the same atoms as everything else: carbon, oxygen, hydrogen, nitrogen and others. In 1828, Friedrich Wöhler, a German chemist, made urea, a chemical from living bodies, out of non-living chemicals. What makes life special is how the atoms are arranged and kept busy.

items.p: Some scientists once said that tiny shapes inside a rock from Mars were fossils of Martian life. Most scientists were not convinced. Why?
opts: Rocks from Mars cannot hold anything
Mars is too far away to study
Ordinary non-living chemistry can make shapes like these, so the shapes alone are not strong evidence
Scientists do not want to find life on Mars
items.why: The rock, called ALH84001, was found in Antarctica. Its shapes could be made without life. Big claims need strong evidence, and a shape is easy to be fooled by.

items.p: A robot is testing Mars soil for life. Sort these results: is each one strong evidence of life, or could ordinary chemistry fool you?
items: gas comes out when sugar water is added
the gas stops when the soil is heated first
tiny cells are seen splitting into two
the gas doubles again and again, as if something is multiplying
the soil fizzes for a minute, then stops
items.a: see items
items.why: Strong evidence is hard for chemistry to fake: cells, multiplying, and a result that heat switches off. Fizzing, colour change and a single burst of gas can all happen without life.

items.p: Every simple definition of life has a tricky case. Match each definition to the case that causes trouble for it.
pairs: 'Living things make young'
A mule
'Living things are always using energy'
A dry seed in a jar
'Anything that grows, uses fuel and gives off waste is alive'
A candle flame
'Anything that carries instructions and makes copies is alive'
A virus
'Anything that senses and moves by itself is alive'
A robot vacuum cleaner
items.a: see pairs
items.why: Each case either breaks a rule while being alive, or fits a rule while not being alive. That is why scientists use many signs together.

items.p: About 8 out of every 100 parts of your own instructions, your DNA, came from viruses that hid inside your ancestors' cells long ago.
items.why: True. Long ago, some viruses slipped their instructions into the cells of our ancestors. Those pieces were copied down the generations. Some now do useful jobs in our bodies. So the line between viruses and us is blurry too.

items.p: In the story 'The Dust in the Gutter', Maria's tiny wheel-animals dried out and woke again and again. Predict: if you dried out a moong seedling with a long root and green leaves, then watered them, would they wake like a dry seed?
opts: Yes, every plant can dry out and wake again
Yes, but only in the dark
No. A sprouted seedling is busy and full of water, so drying out usually kills them
They would turn back into a seed
items.why: A seed gets ready to dry out before they leave the plant. Once they sprout, their cells are busy and lose that power. Being dormant is a special skill, not something every living thing can do.

items.p: A forest fire spreads, uses up dry leaves and leaves ash behind. A goat walking through the same forest also eats dry leaves and leaves droppings behind. Write two ways the fire and the goat are alike, and two ways they are different.
items.a: Alike: both use up leaves as fuel or food, and both join it with oxygen and give out carbon dioxide and waste. Different: the goat is made of cells and the fire is not. The goat releases energy slowly in controlled steps, and the fire all at once. The goat can have a kid who gets her instructions, but a new fire gets no instructions from the old one.
items.why: A strong answer finds real likenesses in the chemistry, then names differences that are signs of life: cells, control, and instructions passed on to young.

items.p: A scientist finds a tiny new speck in a hot spring. Nobody knows whether the speck is alive. Choose three tests from this unit to try first. For each one, say what result would make you think 'alive'.
items.a: For example: 1. Look under a microscope for cells; alive if I see cells. 2. Give the specks warm sugar water; alive if gas starts slowly and keeps growing, and stops if the specks were boiled first. 3. Put a few in fresh water with food; alive if there are more of them the next day, made by the specks themselves and not only inside other cells.
items.why: A strong answer uses tests from the unit (cells, feeding with a boiled comparison, making copies), says what result would count, and does not trust a single sign alone.

items.p: Antoine Lavoisier, a French scientist in the 1780s, said that breathing is a slow burning. Give one way he was right, and one way your cells are different from a flame.
items.a: He was right that both join fuel with oxygen and give out carbon dioxide, water and heat. But a flame does it all at once and has no cells. My cells do it in many small, controlled steps, with instructions controlling each one.
items.why: A strong answer names what is the same, the chemistry, and what is different: speed, control and instructions.

items.p: Draw a long line. Write 'clearly alive' at one end and 'clearly not alive' at the other. Place these on it: a tree, a dry seed, a tun, a virus, a candle flame, a robot, a stone. Next to the two hardest ones, write why you put them there.
items.a: For example: tree and dry seed near 'alive', tun close by, virus in the middle, flame and robot near 'not alive', stone at the end. The virus and the tun are often the hardest.
items.why: There is no single right drawing. A strong answer gives a reason for each hard case, using the signs of life each case shows and lacks.

experiments.title: Sleeping Seeds: is a dry seed alive?
experiments.question: Is a dry seed alive, even though they do nothing? What do they need to wake up?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. What will happen to seeds on wet cotton? To pebbles on wet cotton? To seeds on dry cotton? Draw your guess for each plate, and say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: To make it fair, keep everything the same except one thing. Use the same plates, the same cotton and the same place. The wet seeds and the wet pebbles test whether water alone makes things grow. The wet seeds and the dry seeds test whether seeds need water. Use 6 seeds, because one seed can be a dud.

materials.item: dry whole moong seeds
small pebbles from a plant pot, about the size of a moong seed (or small buttons or beads)
3 small steel plates or saucers
cotton wool or tissue
water in a cup
a ruler
a hand lens

experiments.safety: Do not eat raw seeds from the experiment. Wash hands after handling them. Keep pebbles away from very small children.

schedule.what: Guess what will happen. Set up the three plates. Draw them.
Check all three plates. Draw what you see. Add a few drops of water to plates 1 and 2.
Check, draw and measure the longest root. Water plates 1 and 2.
Check, draw and measure. Water plates 1 and 2.
Last check. Finish the table. Say what you think, what you saw and why.

experiments.record: Fill in the table each day. Draw the three plates side by side each day. On the last day, draw a line chart of the longest root on plate 1, one point for each day.
experiments.context: This is the sleeping seeds experiment. You put dry seeds and pebbles on wet cotton, and more dry seeds on dry cotton, and watch for five days.
