example_chart.title: Made-up example results: the longest moong root on wet cotton
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Three steel plates in a row, each with a layer of cotton: plate 1 wet with six moong seeds, plate 2 wet with six small pebbles, plate 3 dry with six moong seeds.
setup.caption: 1. Make three plates: wet seeds, wet pebbles, dry seeds.

setup.art: A child adding drops of water from a spoon onto the cotton of the first two plates.
setup.caption: 2. Keep plates 1 and 2 damp every day. Leave plate 3 dry.

setup.art: The first plate on day 4, with white roots curling out of the seeds and a ruler laid beside the longest root.
setup.caption: 3. Each day, draw all three plates and measure the longest root.

flow.do: Put a dry moong seed and a pebble side by side on your child's palm.
flow.say: Look at these two. Both are hard, both are still, both do nothing. One of them is alive. Which one, do you think? How could we test it?
flow.kid: Look at the seed and the pebble. Both do nothing. Which one is alive? How could you test it?

ask.q: How could we find out which one is alive?
good: Give them both water and see which one grows.
Watch them for a few days.

flow.context: This is the start of the sleeping seeds experiment. It asks whether a dry seed is alive, even though they do nothing.

flow.do: Help your child draw three plates and their guesses for each.
flow.say: Here is our plan. Plate 1: seeds on wet cotton. Plate 2: pebbles on wet cotton. Plate 3: seeds on dry cotton. What will happen on each plate? Draw your guess.
flow.kid: Draw three plates. Seeds on wet cotton. Pebbles on wet cotton. Seeds on dry cotton. Draw what you think will happen.

flow.do: 1. Put a layer of cotton on each plate. 2. Wet the cotton on plates 1 and 2 until damp but not swimming. 3. Leave plate 3 dry. 4. Put 6 seeds on plate 1, 6 pebbles on plate 2 and 6 seeds on plate 3. 5. Put the plates side by side, away from direct sun.
flow.say: We use two plates of seeds, so the only difference is the water. And we put pebbles on wet cotton, to check that water alone does not make things grow.
flow.kid: Put cotton on three plates. Wet plates 1 and 2. Keep plate 3 dry. Add seeds, pebbles and seeds. Put them side by side.
flow.parent: Cotton should be damp, like a squeezed sponge. Too much water can make seeds rot.

check.q: Why do we put pebbles on wet cotton too?
options: To check that water alone does not make things grow
check.why: The pebbles are a comparison. If pebbles stayed the same and the seeds grew, then something inside the seeds, not the water, made the difference. Picking 'pebbles are alive' is the very idea we are testing.

flow.do: Each day for four days, check all three plates. Draw them. Add a few drops of water to plates 1 and 2. Measure the longest root on plate 1.
flow.say: Let's check our plates. What has changed? Which plate looks different? Let's measure the longest root.
flow.kid: Check your plates. What has changed? Draw them. Measure the longest root.
flow.wait: Come back each day for four days.
flow.parent: Expect seeds on plate 1 to swell within a day. A white root usually appears on day 1 or 2, then a shoot. Pebbles and dry seeds stay the same. Use the hand lens to look at the root tip.

flow.do: On the last day, add water to plate 3, the dry seeds. Talk about what will happen next.
flow.say: Plate 3 has been dry all this time. Were those seeds dead, or still waiting? Let's give them water and see.
flow.kid: Plate 3 was dry all week. Are its seeds dead or waiting? Give them water. Check tomorrow.

check.q: The dry seeds did nothing all week. Then you gave them water, and next day they swelled up. What does this show?
options: They were dead and water brought them back to life
They were alive all along, resting until water came
check.why: The seeds were dormant: alive but resting. Their life processes went on very slowly all week. Picking 'dead and brought back' is how most people first explain it. But water can never bring dead things back to life. The pebbles show that.

flow.do: Ask your child to say or write three short sentences: what I think, what I saw, and why.
flow.say: Now tell me what you found. What do you think now about dry seeds? What did you see that shows it? And why do you think it happened?
flow.kid: Now say or write three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: This is called claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer sounds like this. What I think: a dry seed is alive, only resting. What I saw: the seeds on wet cotton grew roots 40 mm long by day 5, but the pebbles on wet cotton did not change. Why: the seed has a baby plant inside that wakes up when the seed gets water.

experiments.title: The Balloon Test: is dried yeast alive?
experiments.question: Dried yeast looks like sand. Is the yeast alive?
experiments.predict: Guess which bottle will blow up its balloon: yeast with warm sugar water, yeast with cold sugar water, or warm sugar water with no yeast. Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Keep everything the same except one thing at a time. Each bottle gets the same amount of water and sugar. Bottles 1 and 2 test whether warmth matters. Bottles 1 and 3 test whether the yeast is what makes the gas.
results_table: Distance round the balloon after 30 minutes (cm)

materials.item: dried yeast (1 small packet, from a grocery or bakery shop)
sugar
3 small empty plastic bottles of the same size
3 balloons
warm water (bath-warm) and cold water from the fridge
a funnel or a rolled paper cone
a piece of string and a ruler

experiments.safety: A grown-up makes the warm water. It must feel like bath water, not hot. Do not drink the mixture.

schedule.what: Set up three bottles. Watch the balloons for 30 minutes. Measure them. Explain what happened.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the three bottles and their balloons after 30 minutes.
experiments.context: This is the balloon test. You put dried yeast in sugar water in a bottle, with a balloon on top, to see if the yeast does anything a living thing does.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: distance round each balloon after 30 minutes
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: Three small plastic bottles in a row labelled 1, 2 and 3, with a spoon of sugar going into each.
setup.caption: 1. Put 2 teaspoons of sugar in each bottle.

setup.art: A grown-up pouring warm water into bottles 1 and 3 and cold water into bottle 2, and a child tipping yeast through a paper cone into bottles 1 and 2.
setup.caption: 2. Add water. Add yeast to bottles 1 and 2 only.

setup.art: Three bottles with balloons stretched over their necks, the balloon on bottle 1 standing up and half full.
setup.caption: 3. Stretch a balloon over each neck. Watch for 30 minutes.

flow.do: Pour a little dried yeast into your child's palm. Let them look at the yeast with the hand lens.
flow.say: This is dried yeast, from the shop. The tiny grains look like sand. Bakers say the yeast is alive. What do you think? How could we test it?
flow.kid: Look at the dried yeast grains with the lens. They look like sand. Are they alive? How could you find out?
flow.context: This is the start of the balloon test. It asks whether dried yeast, which looks like sand, is alive.

flow.do: 1. Put 2 teaspoons of sugar in each bottle. 2. A grown-up pours half a cup of warm water into bottles 1 and 3. 3. The grown-up pours half a cup of cold water into bottle 2. 4. Add 1 teaspoon of yeast to bottles 1 and 2 only. 5. Swirl each bottle. 6. Stretch a balloon over each neck.
flow.say: Bottle 1 has yeast and warm water. Bottle 2 has yeast and cold water. Bottle 3 has warm water and no yeast. Which balloon do you think will blow up?
flow.kid: Put sugar in all three bottles. A grown-up adds water. Add yeast to bottles 1 and 2. Swirl. Put on the balloons.
flow.parent: Warm means bath-warm, about as warm as your wrist can comfortably hold. Water that is too hot can kill the yeast.

flow.do: Watch the bottles for 30 minutes. Check at 10 minutes and at 30 minutes. Look for bubbles and froth.
flow.say: Let's look at the bottles. Do you see bubbles? Froth? Is any balloon standing up? Living things take in food and give off waste. What could the gas be?
flow.kid: Look at the bottles. Do you see bubbles? Is a balloon filling up? Check again in a while.
flow.parent: Bottle 1 should froth and its balloon should slowly stand up and fill. Bottle 2 will be slow. Bottle 3 will not change. The gas is carbon dioxide, the same gas you breathe out. If the balloon on bottle 1 is still small at 30 minutes, leave it for another half hour. If nothing at all happens, the yeast may be old: try a fresh packet.

flow.do: Wrap a string around the middle of each balloon. Measure the string against the ruler.
flow.say: Let's measure how big each balloon got. Wrap the string around its fattest part, then hold it on the ruler.
flow.kid: Wrap the string round each balloon. Measure the string with the ruler. Write it down.

check.q: Only the yeast bottles made gas. What does this tell us about dried yeast?
options: Yeast cells are alive: they were resting, and in warm sugar water they ate sugar and gave off gas
check.why: Yeast is a tiny fungus. Dried yeast is dormant. In warm sugar water the yeast wakes, eats sugar and breathes out carbon dioxide gas, which fills the balloon. Bottle 3 had sugar and no yeast, and made no gas. So 'sugar makes gas by itself' does not fit the evidence.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: Now tell me what you found. What do you think now about the yeast? What did you see? And why do you think it happened? Why was bottle 2 so slow?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why. Why was the cold bottle slow?
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: dried yeast is alive but resting. What I saw: the warm yeast balloon grew to 30 cm round, but the no-yeast balloon stayed at 10 cm. Why: the yeast woke up, ate the sugar and gave off gas. Cold slows living things down.

experiments.title: The Crystal Garden: it grows, but is it alive?
experiments.question: Salt crystals grow. Does that make them alive?
experiments.predict: Guess what will happen to a thread hanging in very salty water, and to one in plain water. Will anything grow? If it does, will it be alive? Say why you think so.
experiments.fair_test: Set up a second jar with plain water and a thread, as a comparison. Keep both jars side by side in the same warm, still place, so the only difference is the salt.
results_table: Salty jar: what you see on the thread
Plain water jar: what you see

materials.item: salt
materials.qty: about 8 big spoons (you will not need all of it)

materials.item: 2 clean glass jars, wide-mouthed if you have them
water from the tap or a filter, at room temperature
cotton thread, 2 pencils and 2 small buttons to weigh down the threads
a hand lens, or a phone camera zoomed in
a ruler
a dark steel plate or a black paper

experiments.safety: Do not drink the salty water. Put the jars where nobody will knock them over.

schedule.what: Make the salty water and the plain water. Hang the threads. Put salty drops on a dark plate. Guess what will happen.
Look at both threads with the hand lens. Draw them.
Look again. Measure the biggest crystal. Draw.
Last look. Compare with the sleeping seeds. Put the crystal on trial with the signs of life.

experiments.record: Draw the thread each time you look. Write the size of the biggest crystal.
experiments.context: This is the crystal garden. You hang a thread in very salty water, and salt crystals slowly grow on it. Then you ask if growing makes something alive.

setup.art: A child stirring salt into a jar of water, spoon by spoon, until some salt stays at the bottom.
setup.caption: 1. Stir salt into water until no more dissolves.

setup.art: A cotton thread tied to a pencil laid across the top of the jar, the thread hanging into the salty water.
setup.caption: 2. Hang a thread from a pencil into the jar. Do the same with plain water.

setup.art: The thread a week later, covered with small white cube-shaped crystals, seen through a hand lens.
setup.caption: 3. Leave the jars still. Look at the threads every two days.

flow.do: Show your child some salt grains through the hand lens.
flow.say: Look at these salt grains. What shape are they? These are crystals. We are going to grow bigger ones. If they grow, are they alive?
flow.kid: Look at salt grains with the lens. What shape are they? We will grow bigger ones. If they grow, are they alive?
flow.context: This is the start of the crystal garden. It asks whether something that grows has to be alive.

flow.do: 1. Pour 1 cup of water into a jar. 2. Stir in salt, one spoon at a time, stirring for a minute after each spoon. Stop when a little salt stays at the bottom however much you stir. 3. Fill the second jar with plain water. 4. Tie a thread to each pencil, with a button on its end. 5. Lay a pencil across each jar so the thread hangs in the water. 6. Leave the jars open, somewhere warm, dry and still, like a shelf near a window. 7. Put a few drops of the salty water on a dark plate, and leave it beside the jars.
flow.say: The water is holding lots of salt, dissolved in it. As the water slowly evaporates into the air, there is less water to hold the salt. So the salt has to come out somewhere. Let's see where it goes.
flow.kid: Stir salt into a jar of water until no more dissolves. Hang a thread in it. Hang another thread in plain water. Leave both jars very still.
flow.parent: Hot water does not help much: salt dissolves almost as well in cold water as in hot. Iodised salt can make the water a little cloudy, which is fine. Leave the jars open, or the water cannot evaporate.

flow.do: On days 3, 5 and 7, look at both threads, and at the dark plate, with the hand lens. Draw them. Measure the biggest crystal.
flow.say: What is on the threads? How are the crystals growing? From inside, or by adding on at the outside?
flow.kid: Look at both threads with the lens. What do you see? Draw it. Measure the biggest crystal.
flow.parent: The drops on the dark plate dry within a day and leave tiny square crystals, so look at them first. On the thread, crystals usually appear in 2 to 4 days and keep growing as the water evaporates. In a damp week, or in the monsoon, it can take up to two weeks. If the thread is still bare on day 7, keep the jar going and check every few days. The plain water thread stays bare. Notice the flat faces and square corners of salt crystals. Salt also creeps up the inside of the jar as a white crust. That is the same thing happening.

flow.do: Put the crystal thread next to the moong seedlings from the sleeping seeds experiment, if you did it. Go through the signs of life one by one.
flow.say: Let's put our crystal on trial. Does it move? Eat? Get energy from food? Sense? Make young? Get rid of waste? Is it made of cells? Now the seedling. What is the difference in how they grew?
flow.kid: Put your crystal on trial. Go through each sign. Then try the seedling. How did each one grow?

check.q: The crystal and the seedling both grew. What is the big difference?
options: The crystal grew by adding salt on the outside. The seedling grew from inside, by turning water and air into new parts
There is no difference, so both are alive
check.why: A crystal grows only by stacking more of the same particles on its outside. A seedling takes in water and air and builds new parts, like a root and leaves, from inside their cells. Picking 'no difference' usually means treating any growing as a sign of life. Growing alone is not enough.

flow.do: Ask for claim, evidence and reasoning.
flow.say: What do you think now: is the crystal alive? What did you see? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Say three things. What I think. What I saw. Why.
flow.parent: A good answer: What I think: the crystal is not alive. What I saw: it grew to about 5 mm, but only salt built up on the outside, and it did nothing else. The plain water thread stayed bare. Why: the salt came out of the water as the water evaporated. The crystal has no cells and takes in no food.

activities.title: The Mystery Tray

materials.item: a tray or a big plate
a pebble, a dry moong seed, a candle (not lit), a fresh leaf, a dry leaf, a spoon of salt, a toy car, a cotton thread, a feather and a slice of bread
3 sheets of paper labelled ALIVE, NOT ALIVE and ONCE ALIVE

activities.safety: Nothing on the tray is eaten. Watch small children with pebbles and seeds.

schedule.what: Look closely at ten things. Sort them into alive, not alive and once alive. Mark the ones you are not sure about.

activities.record: Take a photo of the sorted tray, or draw it. Put a question mark on every thing you were not sure about.
activities.context: This is a noticing activity. Your child looks closely at ten everyday things on a tray and sorts them into alive, not alive and once alive, before learning anything.

setup.art: A steel tray holding a pebble, a dry moong seed, an unlit candle, a green leaf, a brown dry leaf, a little heap of salt, a toy car, a cotton thread, a feather and a slice of bread.
setup.caption: 1. Put ten everyday things on a tray.

setup.art: A child looking at a dry seed through a hand lens, with three paper labels on the floor: ALIVE, NOT ALIVE and ONCE ALIVE.
setup.caption: 2. Look closely. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

setup.art: The ten things sorted onto the three labels, with small paper question marks on the seed, the candle and the bread.
setup.caption: 3. Sort them. Put a question mark on the hard ones.

flow.do: Put the tray in front of your child. Do not explain anything yet.
flow.say: Here are ten things from our home. Look very closely at each one. What do you notice? What do you wonder about?
flow.kid: Look closely at each thing on the tray. What do you notice? What do you wonder?

good: The seed looks like a tiny pebble.
The leaf is still green.
The bread has holes in it.

flow.context: This is the start of the Mystery Tray. Your child looks at ten everyday things before sorting them.

flow.do: Lay the three labels on the floor. Your child sorts each thing onto one label.
flow.say: Put each thing on a label: alive, not alive, or once alive. Once alive means it was part of a living thing, but is not alive now. Put a question mark on any you are not sure about.
flow.kid: Sort each thing. Alive, not alive, or once alive. Once alive means it used to be part of something living. Mark the hard ones with a question mark.
flow.parent: Do not correct anything yet. Most children put the seed with the pebble, and many put the candle near 'alive' because it can burn. Both are perfect puzzles for this unit. Bread is made from wheat, which was alive, and it holds yeast that was alive.

flow.do: Pick up the seed and the pebble. Then the candle.
flow.say: Which ones were hardest? Why? What would you need to see to be sure the seed is alive? What would you need to see to be sure the candle is not?
flow.kid: Which ones were hard? What test could prove the seed is alive?

check.q: Which thing on the tray is alive right now, even though it does nothing?
check.why: The dry seed is alive but resting. Give them water and they grow a root. A pebble never can. Picking the toy car usually means 'it can move, so it might be alive'. But moving alone tells us nothing.

flow.think: Keep your tray. At the end of this unit, sort it again. Will you change anything?

activities.title: Put the Candle on Trial

materials.item: a short candle on a steel plate, shorter than the glass tumbler
a matchbox (grown-up only)
a clear glass tumbler
2 steel spoons, cooled in the fridge for 10 minutes
a second, unlit candle
the sign cards from the game, or a list of the signs of life

activities.safety: A grown-up lights and handles the candle and the hot spoon the whole time. Children stay an arm's length from the flame and never reach over it. Tie back long hair and tuck in dupattas and loose sleeves. Keep paper and cloth away, and keep a cup of water nearby. Put the flame out at the end, and let the tumbler and the spoon cool before anyone touches them.

schedule.what: Test the candle flame against each sign of life. Decide: alive or not?

activities.record: Draw a two-column chart: 'Signs the flame showed' and 'Signs it lacked'. Write your verdict at the bottom.
activities.context: This is a trial. A grown-up lights a candle, and together you test the flame against each sign of life to decide if fire is alive.

setup.art: A grown-up lighting a small candle on a steel plate, with a glass tumbler and a steel spoon beside it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up lights a candle on a steel plate.

setup.art: A grown-up holding a cold steel spoon over a candle flame, with a little mist on the spoon and a black smudge of soot where it touched the flame tip.
setup.caption: 2. Hold a cold spoon over the flame. Look for mist, then soot.

setup.art: A glass tumbler placed over the candle, the flame shrinking to a tiny blue dot.
setup.caption: 3. Cover the candle with a glass. Watch the flame.

flow.do: A grown-up lights the candle. Everyone sits back an arm's length away.
flow.say: Today the flame is on trial. We will test it, sign by sign. Does it move? Watch it. Does it grow? Watch it for a minute after it is lit.
flow.kid: A grown-up lights the candle. Sit back. Watch the flame. Does it move? Does it change?
flow.context: This is the start of the candle trial. You test a candle flame against the signs of life.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up holds a cold spoon by its handle, about three finger-widths above the flame, for 2 seconds. Look straight away: the mist fades in a few seconds as the spoon warms. 2. Then the grown-up holds the same spoon in the very tip of the flame for 2 seconds, and shows the black soot. 3. Everyone holds a palm about a hand-length from the side of the flame, never above it. Then everyone puts their palms on their own cheeks. 4. Your child breathes on the second cold spoon.
flow.say: Look at the spoon. The mist is water that the flame made. The black smudge is soot, from wax that did not burn completely. Now feel the flame's warmth, then feel your own cheeks. You are warm too. Breathe on this cold spoon. What do you see?
flow.kid: Look at the spoon. The flame made mist and black soot. Feel the warm flame. Feel your warm cheeks. Breathe on a cold spoon. What do you see?
flow.parent: The spoon gets hot in the flame, so hold it by the far end of the handle, and put it down on the steel plate to cool before anyone touches it. Wipe off the soot afterwards. If you see no mist, the spoon was not cold enough: cool it again and look more quickly. Both the flame and your child's breath mist the spoon, and both give out warmth. Let your child notice this. The explanation comes later.

flow.do: A grown-up puts the glass tumbler gently over the candle. Watch until the flame goes out.
flow.say: What do you think will happen to the flame under the glass? Why do you think so? Now watch. Afterwards: what did the flame need that ran out?
flow.kid: What will happen to the flame under the glass? Guess first. Then watch. What ran out?

check.q: Why did the flame go out under the glass?
options: The glass made it too dark
It used up some of the oxygen under the glass, and too little was left
check.why: A flame needs oxygen, a gas in the air. Under the glass it used up some of the oxygen and could not get more. When too little was left, it went out. Picking 'finished its wax' is a fair guess, but the candle still has plenty of wax. The flame went out because the glass cut off the air.

flow.do: A grown-up lights the candle again. Then the grown-up holds the second candle and touches its wick to the flame for a moment.
flow.say: Look. One flame has made a new flame. Is that like a cat having kittens? Does the new flame carry anything from the first one, the way kittens get instructions from their mother?
flow.kid: Watch. One flame lights another. Is that like a baby? Does the new flame get anything from the old one?

ask.q: Is the new flame like the old one's baby?
good: No. The new flame looks the way it does because of its own wax and wick, not because of the old flame.
Kittens get instructions from their mother. A new flame gets no instructions from the old one.

flow.do: Blow out both candles. Fill in the two-column chart together.
flow.say: Let's sum up the trial. Which signs did the flame show? Which did it lack? Did it have cells? Did it pass on instructions? So, what is your verdict?
flow.kid: Fill in your chart. Signs the flame showed. Signs it lacked. Then give your verdict: alive or not alive?
flow.parent: A good verdict: 'Not alive. The flame moved, grew, used fuel and oxygen, made waste and started a new flame. But it has no cells and passes on no instructions.' If your child says it is a little bit alive, ask what it would need to be fully alive. Then ask: the flame and you both made the spoon misty and both felt warm. Why might that be?

activities.title: Water Bear Hunt (if you can find moss)

materials.item: a small clump of dry moss from a wall, a tree trunk or the soil of an old plant pot
a small bowl or a saucer of rainwater or bottled water
a clear plastic lid or a steel plate with a dark bottom
a dropper or a straw
a phone microscope clip, or a strong hand lens

activities.safety: A grown-up goes with you to collect moss. Take only a thumb-sized clump. Wash hands afterwards. Never touch your eyes while handling moss.

schedule.what: Collect a small clump of dry moss. Put the clump in a bowl of water overnight.
Squeeze the moss water onto a dark plate. Search for tiny eight-legged animals with a lens or a phone microscope.

activities.record: Draw everything that moves. If you find a water bear, count their legs and draw how they walk.
activities.context: This is a hunt for water bears, the tiny eight-legged animals that can dry out and wake up again. You soak dry moss in water and search the water for them.

setup.art: A grown-up and a child gently pulling a thumb-sized clump of dry moss from an old brick wall.
setup.caption: 1. With a grown-up, collect a small clump of dry moss.

setup.art: The clump of moss soaking in a small bowl of water on a windowsill overnight.
setup.caption: 2. Soak the moss in water overnight. The water bears wake up.

setup.art: A phone with a clip-on microscope lens held over a dark plate with drops of moss water, and on the screen a chubby eight-legged water bear.
setup.caption: 3. Squeeze the moss onto a dark plate. Search with a lens.

flow.do: With your child, find moss growing on a wall, a tree trunk or a roof. Take one thumb-sized clump. At home, put the clump in a bowl of water overnight.
flow.say: This moss is dry, and so are any water bears living there. They have curled into tiny dry balls called tuns. If we give them water tonight, they may wake up by tomorrow.
flow.kid: Find some dry moss with a grown-up. Take a small clump. Put the clump in water overnight. Any water bears in there may wake up.
flow.context: This is the start of the water bear hunt. You collect dry moss and soak the clump.

flow.do: Next day, squeeze the moss over the dark plate. Use the dropper to spread the water in small drops. Search each drop slowly with the phone microscope or lens.
flow.say: Water bears are about as long as a grain of salt is wide. Look for a slow, chubby animal that waddles on eight stumpy legs. Be patient. Many hunters look for a long time.
flow.kid: Squeeze the moss onto the plate. Look at each drop slowly. Look for a chubby animal with eight short legs.
flow.parent: Water bears are common but tiny, about half a millimetre long. With a hand lens you may only see a slowly moving speck. A phone microscope clip of 30 times or more helps a lot. You will probably also see other tiny moss animals, like wriggling rotifers. They can dry out and wake again too. Finding nothing is normal. Try moss from another place, and watch the water bear video in this unit to see one walking.

flow.do: Talk about what you found, even if it was not a water bear.
flow.say: Yesterday this moss was dry and nothing moved in there. Today there may be tiny animals swimming. Were they dead yesterday? Or waiting?
flow.kid: Did anything move in the water? Yesterday the moss was dry. Were those animals dead, or waiting?

check.q: Tiny animals swim in the water from dry moss. Where did they come from?
options: The water made them out of nothing
They were in the dry moss all along, resting, and woke up in the water
They hatched from the moss leaves
check.why: They were in the moss all along, dried out and resting. Water woke them. Picking 'the water made them' is the old idea of spontaneous generation. Scientists showed long ago that living things only come from other living things.

activities.title: Act It Out: A Day in the Life of a Virus

materials.item: a cardboard box with a door cut in one side (the cell)
about 20 building blocks or folded paper squares (the cell's building parts)
a folded paper with 'Make more of me' written on it (the virus's instructions)
a paper cap or a bowl as the virus coat

activities.safety: Clear a space so nobody trips.

schedule.what: Act out a virus outside a cell and inside a cell. Talk about whether viruses are alive.

activities.record: Draw a comic in three boxes: the virus drifting, the virus getting in, and the cell making copies.
activities.context: This is a drama game. One person plays a virus and one plays a living cell, to show how a virus can only make copies inside a cell.

setup.art: A cardboard box with a small door, labelled CELL, full of building blocks, and a child holding a folded paper labelled MAKE MORE OF ME.
setup.caption: 1. The box is the cell. The paper note is the virus's instructions.

setup.art: A child in a paper cap standing very still in the middle of a room, labelled VIRUS OUTSIDE A CELL.
setup.caption: 2. The virus stands still. Alone, they cannot make copies.

setup.art: A parent inside the 'cell' reading the note and quickly building many small paper copies of the virus.
setup.caption: 3. Inside the cell, the cell reads the note and builds copies.

flow.do: Your child wears the paper cap and holds the note. Ask them to try to do the signs of life alone: eat, grow, move by themselves.
flow.say: You are a virus now. You are a tiny packet of instructions in a coat. Outside a cell, a virus does not eat or grow. So stand very still. The wind carries you, until you meet a cell.
flow.kid: You are a virus. You are only a note in a coat. Alone, you can't eat or grow. Stand still. The wind carries you.
flow.context: This is the start of the virus drama. Your child plays a virus floating outside a cell.

flow.do: The parent is the cell, sitting by the box full of blocks. Your child drifts to the box and pushes the note through the door.
flow.say: Now you bump into a living cell. You slip your instructions inside. The cell reads them, just as they read their own.
flow.kid: You drift to the cell. Push your note through the door. The cell reads it.
flow.parent: Read the note aloud, slowly and clearly: 'Make more of me.'

flow.do: The parent uses the blocks to build small 'virus' shapes for one minute, as many as possible. Then the parent pushes them out of the door.
flow.say: Look. The cell is using their own building parts and their own energy to make copies of you. You did not do any of the work. Now the new viruses burst out to find more cells.
flow.kid: Watch the cell build copies of you. They do all the work. Now the copies burst out.

good: The cell did.
The cell used their own parts and energy.

flow.do: Sit down together and talk.
flow.say: So, is a virus alive? They cannot do anything alone. But they make copies of themselves, and they change over time. Scientists still argue. What do you think?
flow.kid: Is a virus alive? They can't do anything alone. But they make copies. What do you think? Why?

check.q: Why do scientists argue about whether viruses are alive?
options: Because viruses are too big to see
Because a virus makes copies of themselves, but only inside a living cell, and does no life processes alone
Because viruses are made of metal
check.why: A virus carries instructions and makes copies, like living things. But they can only do this inside a cell, and alone they make no copies. That is why they sit on the edge. Picking 'animals' is a common mix-up. Viruses have no cells at all, while every animal is made of many cells.

activities.title: Is My Toy Robot Alive?

materials.item: a battery toy that moves or makes sounds, or a phone
a pet, a houseplant or a potted tulsi plant to compare
paper and pencil

activities.safety: Do not open battery boxes. Be gentle with pets.

schedule.what: Test a toy against the signs of life. Compare it with a living thing. Design what it would need to be alive.

activities.record: Make a table with two columns, the toy and the living thing, and a tick or cross for each sign.
activities.context: This activity puts a moving toy or a phone on trial against the signs of life, and compares it with a pet or a plant.

setup.art: A battery toy car and a potted tulsi plant side by side on a table, with a blank two-column table on paper.
setup.caption: 1. Put a moving toy next to a living thing.

setup.art: A child ticking boxes on the table with a pencil while the toy car moves.
setup.caption: 2. Test each sign of life for both.

setup.art: A child's drawing of a robot with extra parts labelled 'grows', 'finds its own food' and 'makes baby robots'.
setup.caption: 3. Draw what the toy would need to be alive.

flow.do: Switch the toy on. Go through each sign of life for the toy, then for the plant or pet.
flow.say: Does the toy move? Sense? Grow? Eat? Get rid of waste? Make young? Is it made of cells? Now let's try the tulsi plant.
flow.kid: Switch on the toy. Does it move, sense, grow, eat or make babies? Now test the plant.
flow.context: This is the start of the robot trial. You test a moving toy against the signs of life.

flow.do: Look at the table together.
flow.say: The toy moves and maybe senses. The plant hardly moves at all, but they tick almost every box. So which is alive? What is the toy missing?
flow.kid: Look at your table. Which has more ticks? What is the toy missing?

check.q: A robot can sense walls and move by itself. Why is it still not alive?
options: Because it has no cells, does not grow or take in food, and cannot make young by itself
check.why: A robot follows instructions people wrote. It has no cells, does not grow, and cannot build a baby robot from food. Picking 'not green' mixes up being a plant with being alive. Animals are not green either, and they are alive.

flow.do: Your child draws a robot with all the extra parts it would need to be alive.
flow.say: Imagine you had to make this toy truly alive. What would you have to add? Draw it.
flow.kid: Draw the toy with everything it would need to be alive.
flow.think: If someone built a robot that could find its own food, repair itself and build copies, would you call it alive?

activities.title: Draw the Line

materials.item: a long piece of string or a dupatta, about 2 metres
two paper signs: SURELY ALIVE and SURELY NOT ALIVE
12 small paper cards: a stone, a crystal, fire, a robot, a cloud, a virus, a dry seed, a water bear in a tun, a bacterium, a mule, a tree and you

activities.safety: Lay the string flat so nobody trips.

schedule.what: Place cards along a line from surely alive to surely not alive. Talk about where the line should go.

activities.record: Take a photo of the line, or draw it. Mark where you would put the edge between alive and not alive.
activities.context: In this activity, the family lays a string across the floor, from 'surely alive' at one end to 'surely not alive' at the other, and places tricky cases along it.

setup.art: A long string across a floor, with a sign SURELY ALIVE at one end and SURELY NOT ALIVE at the other.
setup.caption: 1. Lay a string across the floor with a sign at each end.

setup.art: A family kneeling along the string, placing small cards: a tree near one end, a stone near the other, and a virus card in the middle.
setup.caption: 2. Everyone places the cards along the line.

setup.art: A child laying a ruler across the string at one point, marking 'the edge'.
setup.caption: 3. Decide: where does alive end? Mark the place.

flow.do: Lay the string out. Give each family member some cards. Take turns placing them along the string.
flow.say: Put each card somewhere along the string. The tree goes right at 'surely alive'. Where does the virus go? The dry seed? The fire?
flow.kid: Put each card along the string. Surely alive at one end. Surely not alive at the other. Where does each card go?
flow.context: This is the start of Draw the Line. Your family places tricky cases along a line from alive to not alive.

flow.do: Look at the cards in the middle. Each person moves one card they disagree with, and says why.
flow.say: Some cards ended up in the middle. Do you agree with where they are? Move one, and tell us why.
flow.kid: Look at the middle of the line. Move one card you disagree with. Say why.
flow.parent: There is no right line. Most families put the virus near the middle. The dry seed often starts near 'not alive' and moves towards 'alive' after the seed experiment. That movement is learning.

flow.do: Ask your child to put a ruler or a pencil across the string where they think 'alive' really begins.
flow.say: If you had to draw one sharp line, where would it go? Is it easy to choose? Why do you think scientists find it hard too?
flow.kid: Put a pencil across the string where 'alive' begins. Was that easy? Why or why not?

check.q: Why is it hard to draw one sharp line between alive and not alive?
options: Because some things, like viruses and dry seeds, have some signs of life but not others
check.why: Tricky cases sit in between. A virus makes copies but only inside a cell. A dry seed shows no signs, yet wakes later. Picking 'scientists have not tried' is not right. They have tried for hundreds of years, and the tricky cases are exactly what they argue about.

projects.title: The Museum of Tricky Cases

materials.item: a big sheet of chart paper or a tray for each exhibit
your crystal thread, sprouted seeds, a candle (unlit), a toy robot and drawings of a virus and a water bear
colour pencils and small paper label cards

projects.safety: Candles stay unlit in the museum.

schedule.what: Choose six tricky cases. Make a label card for each: signs it shows, signs it lacks, and a verdict.
Set up the museum. Give a tour to the family. Answer their questions.

projects.record: Keep the label cards. Take photos of the museum.
projects.context: In this project your child builds a small home museum of tricky cases, like fire, a crystal and a virus, with a label for each, and gives a tour.

setup.art: Six exhibits on a table: a crystal on a thread, a plate of moong sprouts, an unlit candle, a toy robot, a drawing of a virus and a drawing of a water bear, each with a folded label card.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out six tricky cases with a label card for each.

setup.art: A close-up label card with three parts: 'Signs I show', 'Signs I lack' and 'Verdict: alive, not alive or argued'.
setup.caption: 2. Fill in each label: signs it shows, signs it lacks, verdict.

setup.art: A child with a paper badge saying GUIDE, pointing at the virus drawing while parents listen.
setup.caption: 3. Give the family a tour and answer their questions.

flow.do: Help your child choose six cases and make a label card for each.
flow.say: A museum label tells visitors the most important things in a few words. For each case, write the signs it shows, the signs it lacks, and your verdict.
flow.kid: Choose six tricky cases. Write the signs it shows. Write the signs it lacks. Then give your verdict.
flow.wait: Finish the labels today. Set up the museum tomorrow.
flow.context: This is the first day of the Museum of Tricky Cases project. Your child makes a label for each exhibit.

flow.do: Set up the exhibits. Your child gives a tour. Each visitor asks one hard question.
flow.say: Welcome to the museum. Please tell us about each exhibit. Which one is the hardest to decide about?
flow.kid: Set up your museum. Give your family a tour. Answer one hard question about each exhibit.
flow.parent: Good hard questions: 'If the virus can make copies, why aren't they alive?' 'If the seed does nothing, how do you know they are alive?' 'Fire makes new fires. Isn't that having babies?'

check.q: A visitor says: 'The crystal grows, so it must be alive.' What is the best reply?
options: Crystals grow by adding on outside. They have no cells and take in no food, so growing alone does not make them alive
check.why: The crystal really does grow, so 'they do not really grow' is wrong. But it grows only by stacking more salt on the outside. Living things grow from inside, using food. 'Only animals grow' forgets plants, which grow all their lives.

challenges.title: Design a Life Detector for Mars
challenges.problem: A robot is going to Mars. It will dig up a spoon of soil. Your job is to design the tests it should do to find out whether anything in the soil is alive.
constraints: The robot can only test a tiny spoon of soil.
No human will be there to look.
The robot must not be fooled by fire, crystals or ordinary chemistry.
materials: a shoebox to build a model robot
3 big spoons of soil from a plant pot, and 3 big spoons of the same soil that a grown-up has heated in a dry pan for 10 minutes
2 small plastic bottles, 2 balloons, sugar and warm water
general: Add water and food, and watch for gas, like the yeast balloon test.
Look through a microscope for cells.
Wait and see whether anything grows from inside or makes more of itself.
creative: Test the soil once, then heat it strongly and test again. If gas stops after heating, something living may have been killed. In 1976 NASA's Viking landers on Mars did tests like this. One test gave a puzzling result, and scientists still argue about what it meant.
Look for instructions, like the molecules inside cells that carry genes.
Test something you know is not alive, like sand, as a comparison. If the sand also 'passes', your test is fooled.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own test. Draw it, and say how it avoids being fooled by fire, crystals and chemistry.
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You design the tests a robot on Mars should do to find out whether anything in a spoon of soil is alive.

setup.art: A model robot made from a shoebox with a spoon arm, scooping red soil on a pretend Mars surface.
setup.caption: 1. Picture the robot digging up a spoon of Mars soil.

setup.art: Two small plastic bottles, one with pot soil and one with heated soil, each with sugar water added and a balloon over the neck.
setup.caption: 2. Practise your test on pot soil and on heated soil.

setup.art: A child's drawing of the robot with three labelled tests: 'add food, watch for gas', 'look for cells', 'heat, then test again'.
setup.caption: 3. Draw your robot's tests, step by step.

flow.do: Read the problem together. List the signs of life your child knows.
flow.say: Our robot is alone on Mars. Which signs of life can it test in a spoon of soil? Which ones are hard to test?
flow.kid: Your robot is alone on Mars. Which signs of life can it test in a spoon of soil?
flow.context: This is the start of the Mars life detector challenge.

flow.do: Practise one test at home. Put 3 big spoons of pot soil in one bottle. Put 3 big spoons of the heated soil in the other. Add 2 teaspoons of sugar and half a cup of warm water to each. Stretch a balloon over each neck. Check the next morning.
flow.say: Soil from a plant pot is full of tiny living things. Heating the soil kills most of them. If our test works, which bottle should make more gas?
flow.kid: Add sugar water to pot soil and to heated soil. Cover both with a balloon. Check tomorrow. Which one made gas?
flow.parent: A grown-up heats the soil in a dry pan, stirring, for about 10 minutes, then lets it cool. The pot soil balloon may only stand up a little, because bacteria and fungi in soil give off only a small amount of carbon dioxide. So also look for tiny bubbles and a sour smell. The heated soil should show much less. If neither bottle changes, the soil may be very dry or old: try soil from a pot that is watered often. This is close to what the Viking landers did on Mars in 1976.

flow.do: Your child draws the robot and its tests, with a way to avoid being fooled.
flow.say: How will your robot be sure it found life, and not just a chemical fizz? Draw your plan.
flow.kid: Draw your robot and its tests. How will it avoid being fooled?

check.q: Why test heated soil next to the fresh soil?
options: As a comparison: if the heated soil passes the test too, the test is fooled by ordinary chemistry
Because heated soil is more alive
check.why: A comparison shows what happens when the living things are killed. If heated soil makes as much gas as fresh soil, the gas probably came from ordinary chemistry, not life. But heat can change some chemicals too. That is one reason scientists still argue about the Viking results. This is like the pebble plate in the sleeping seeds experiment. Picking 'heated soil is more alive' is the opposite of the idea.

challenges.title: Keep a Seed Asleep for a Year
challenges.problem: A farmer wants to save her best seeds for next year's sowing. Design a way to keep them asleep, so they do not sprout or rot, but still wake up next year.
constraints: Use only things found at home.
The seeds must still sprout after storage.
No chemicals that could harm people or animals.
general: Dry the seeds well in the sun first, because water wakes them up.
Store them in an airtight jar, so damp air cannot get in.
Keep the jar somewhere cool and dark.
creative: Many Indian farmers store grain with dried neem leaves to keep insects away.

quiz.p: Ammu, a girl in Class 3, says: 'A mushroom has no legs and no eyes, and stays in one place. So a mushroom is not alive.' Which fact shows that Ammu is wrong?
opts: The mushroom is soft
The mushroom grows from inside and makes spores that grow into new mushrooms
The mushroom is a different colour from the soil
The mushroom grows near trees
quiz.why: Growing from inside and making young are strong signs of life. Softness, colour and place tell you nothing. A strong answer tests the mushroom against several signs, not just moving.

quiz.p: A cloud moves, grows bigger and splits into smaller clouds. Which sign of life does a cloud NOT have?
opts: Being made of cells
Moving
Growing bigger
Splitting into more
quiz.why: A cloud is tiny drops of water pushed by the wind. It moves, grows and splits, but has no cells and passes on no instructions.

quiz.p: Sugar crystals can grow on a thread hung in thick sugar syrup. Is a growing sugar crystal alive?
opts: Yes, because the crystal grows
No. The crystal grows only by sugar sticking onto the outside
Yes, because sugar is food
Only while the crystal is growing
quiz.why: Living things grow from inside, by turning food into new parts. A crystal only adds on outside, just like the salt crystals in the crystal garden.

quiz.p: Your cells and a candle flame both join fuel with oxygen to release energy. Why don't you catch fire?
opts: Your cells release the energy slowly, in many small controlled steps
There is no oxygen inside you
Your body is too wet to burn
Food is not a fuel
quiz.why: Both use the same chemistry. The difference is speed and control. Your cells release a little energy at a time, so you stay warm and never burn.

quiz.p: A dried water bear can stay alive for years with almost no water in their body.
quiz.why: True. A dried water bear, called a tun, is dormant. When water comes back, they uncurl and walk again.

quiz.p: Dried yeast in a packet looks like sand. In the balloon test, the bottles with yeast filled their balloons with gas. What does this show about the yeast in the packet?
opts: The yeast in the packet were dead
The packet itself makes gas
The yeast were alive but dormant, and woke up in the warm sugar water
Sand makes gas in water
quiz.why: Dormant means alive but resting. The yeast fed on the sugar and gave off gas. The bottle without yeast made none.

quiz.p: A flu virus gets inside a cell in your nose. Then many new flu viruses come out. Who did the work of building the new viruses?
opts: The virus, using food they carried with them
The cell, which followed the virus's instructions
The air in your nose
Nobody. The new viruses grew by themselves, like a crystal
quiz.why: A virus carries instructions but has no cell of their own. The cell they get into reads those instructions and builds the copies. This is why scientists argue about whether viruses are alive.

quiz.p: Why do scientists still argue about whether viruses are alive?
opts: Nobody has ever seen a virus
Viruses carry instructions and evolve, but do nothing at all outside a living cell
Viruses are bigger than animals
Viruses are made of salt
quiz.why: Viruses have some signs of life and lack others. That is why they sit right on the edge. Scientists have seen them, using electron microscopes.

quiz.p: A talking toy says hello when you clap and flaps its paper wings. Which is the best reason the talking toy is not alive?
opts: It has no cells, takes in no food, does not grow and cannot make young
It is too small
It only says one word
It was bought in a shop
quiz.why: The toy senses a clap and moves, but those are only two signs. A real bird does all the signs of life together.

quiz.p: Tanvi, a girl in Class 4, wants to test whether dry chana from the kitchen is alive. She puts chana on wet cotton. What should she put on a second plate to make her test fair?
opts: Beads or pebbles of the same size on wet cotton, to see if water alone changes anything
More chana on a plate with no cotton
Nothing, one plate is enough
Chana fried in oil
quiz.why: The second plate is the comparison. Both plates get the same water. If only the chana grows, the chana's own life made the difference, just like the pebble plate in the sleeping seeds experiment.

quiz.p: In claim, evidence and reasoning, the evidence is what you saw. Which of these is evidence from the balloon test?
opts: I think yeast is alive
Living things feed and give off waste
Bakers use yeast to make bread
The balloon on the warm yeast bottle grew big, but the balloon on the bottle without yeast stayed flat
quiz.why: Evidence is a result you saw or measured. 'I think yeast is alive' is the claim. 'Living things feed and give off waste' is the reasoning.

quiz.p: Why is it so hard to draw one sharp line between alive and not alive?
opts: Some cases, like viruses and tuns, show some signs of life but not others
Scientists have never tried to draw it
Living things keep changing colour
Every case is easy once you look closely
quiz.why: Most things are clearly on one side: trees are alive and stones are not. The hard part is the edge, where viruses and dormant things sit.

quiz.p: Scientists have made some of the building blocks of life from gases in a lab, but nobody yet knows how the first living thing began.
quiz.why: True. In 1952, Stanley Miller and Harold Urey made some building blocks of life from gases and sparks. But how the first living thing began is still an open question.

applications: Farmers and seed banks store seeds dry and cool, so they stay dormant and alive for years.
Bakers use dried yeast that wakes up in warm water and makes bread dough rise.
Doctors and scientists make vaccines by studying how viruses get into cells.
Scientists who study water bears hope to learn how to store medicines and vaccines dry, without a fridge.
NASA and other space agencies design robots and tests to search for signs of life on Mars and other worlds.
Food is kept in the fridge because cold slows down the bacteria and fungi that spoil it.
Dried fruits and papad last long because, without water, germs cannot grow well. Pickles last because of salt, oil and sourness.
Fire fighters use the 'fire needs fuel, air and heat' idea. Take away one, and the fire dies.
Viruses that attack only bacteria, called phages, are being tested as medicines against infections.
Engineers build robots that copy living things, like walking, grasping or finding their way.

open_questions.why_open: It depends on how you define life. Viruses do some things living things do but not others, and scientists have not agreed on a definition.

open_questions.q: How did the first living thing come from non-living chemicals?
open_questions.why_open: It happened about 4 billion years ago and left no clear traces. Experiments have made some building blocks, but no one has made life from scratch.

open_questions.q: Is a dried water bear alive while they are dry, or is it in a third state?
open_questions.why_open: Their life processes are so slow they are very hard to measure. Scientists argue about whether anything at all is happening inside.

open_questions.q: Is there life on other planets or moons, like Mars, Europa or Enceladus?
open_questions.why_open: We have only one example of life, on Earth. Missions are searching, but nothing has been found for sure yet.

open_questions.q: Could a machine or a computer program ever be alive?
open_questions.why_open: Some programs copy themselves and change, and some machines can repair themselves. Whether that counts as life depends on whether life must be made of cells and chemistry.

open_questions.q: How long can a seed stay dormant and still wake?
open_questions.why_open: Seeds of about 1,300 years old have grown. Nobody knows the true limit, and different seeds are very different.

open_questions.q: What is it like to be a plant?
open_questions.why_open: Plants feel. They sense touch, light, heat and damage, and J.C. Bose measured the electrical signals they send. What a plant's feeling is like from the inside is still a question nobody has answered.

maths.problem: In the sleeping seeds experiment, 6 moong seeds went on wet cotton. By day 5, 5 of them had grown a root. What fraction of the seeds woke up?
maths.answer: 5 out of 6, which is five sixths.
maths.explain: There were 6 seeds in all. 5 of them grew a root. So 5 out of 6 woke up. We write this as the fraction five sixths. Only 1 seed out of 6 did not wake. That one may have died, or may need more time.
maths.context: This is about the sleeping seeds experiment, where you put 6 dry moong seeds on wet cotton and watched which ones grew a root.
maths.why_maths: Seed banks test stored seeds this way. A fraction tells them how many of their seeds are still alive.

maths.problem: Look at the chart of the longest moong root. On day 3 it was 12 mm long. On day 5 it was 40 mm long. How much did it grow in those two days?
maths.explain: On day 5 the root was 40 mm. On day 3 it was 12 mm. 40 take away 12 is 28. So the root grew 28 mm in two days. That is about 14 mm each day.

chart.title: The longest moong root on wet cotton (made-up example)

maths.context: This is about the sleeping seeds experiment. You measured the longest root on the wet cotton plate every day.
maths.why_maths: Taking one measurement from another shows how fast something grew. Fast growth from inside is a sign of a living thing waking up.

maths.problem: In the balloon test, the string round the warm yeast balloon measured 30 cm. The string round the no-yeast balloon measured 10 cm. How many times bigger round was the yeast balloon?
maths.explain: The yeast balloon was 30 cm round. The no-yeast balloon was 10 cm round. 30 divided by 10 is 3. So the yeast balloon was 3 times as big round. You can check: 10 + 10 + 10 = 30.

chart.title: Distance round each balloon after 30 minutes (made-up example)

maths.context: This is about the balloon test, where you put dried yeast in warm sugar water with a balloon on top, next to a bottle with no yeast.
maths.why_maths: Saying 'three times bigger' tells us how strong the effect of the living yeast was, compared with the bottle without yeast.

maths.problem: In the candle trial, you tested the flame against the 9 sign cards. It showed 5 of them: it moved, took in wax as fuel, got energy from it, grew and made waste. How many signs did it not show?
maths.explain: There were 9 signs in all. The flame showed 5. 9 take away 5 is 4. The 4 it did not show were sensing, making young, being made of cells and passing on instructions. The last two are the ones that matter most.
maths.context: This is about the candle trial, where a grown-up lit a candle and you tested the flame against each sign of life.
maths.why_maths: Counting the signs a thing shows and lacks helps us compare tricky cases fairly, instead of guessing.

maths.problem: In the crystal garden, the biggest crystal was 2 mm on day 3, 4 mm on day 5 and 6 mm on day 7. If it keeps growing the same way, how big will it be on day 9?
maths.explain: Every two days, the crystal grew 2 mm: 2, then 4, then 6. The pattern adds 2 each time. So on day 9 it will be 6 + 2 = 8 mm. In real life the crystal will stop when the water dries up or the salt runs out.
maths.context: This is about the crystal garden, where salt crystals grew on a thread hanging in salty water, and you measured the biggest one.
maths.why_maths: Finding a pattern in measurements lets scientists predict what will happen next, and then test whether they were right.

roots.context: We have tested tricky cases against the signs of life: fire, a salt crystal, a robot, a dry seed, a water bear and a virus. Now we ask what fire, the most famous tricky case, tells us about our own bodies.

deep_truth.truth: A cold spoon mists over when held above a candle flame, and when you breathe on it. The flame and your cells both join fuel with oxygen, and give out heat and water. The flame does it all at once, and your cells do it slowly, in many small steps. So you need to breathe for the same reason a candle needs air.
deep_truth.habit: We think living things run on some special life-stuff that fire, rocks and machines lack. People called this idea vitalism. But your cells free their energy by the same kind of change as a flame.
deep_truth.evidence: In the candle trial, the flame needed air, gave out warmth and misted a cold spoon, just as your body and breath did. In 1783 Lavoisier and Laplace found that a guinea pig's body heat was close to the heat from burning charcoal that made the same amount of carbon dioxide.

three.who_am_i: You are warm because your cells join food with oxygen, the same change that makes a flame hot. You are made of the same kinds of atoms as rocks, air and stars.
three.what_is_life: Scientists find no special chemicals in living things. A cell is alive because of how their ordinary chemistry is organised, kept going and passed on.
three.what_is_this_world: Living and non-living things are made of the same atoms and use the same chemistry. All of them are part of one consciousness, each aware in its own way.

roots.thread: A flame, a crystal, a virus and you are made of the same few kinds of atoms, and a flame and your cells do the same chemistry. Everything comes from one source, consciousness, and shows up as many different things. Some of them, like you, are arranged into cells that keep themselves going and pass on instructions, and biologists call them alive. A flame or a crystal is not alive by those tests, but it is still aware in its own way. Being alive and being aware are two different questions.

teachings.teaching: This old book of Ayurveda says there is a fire in the body, called agni, that turns food into the body. It says a person's life, strength and warmth depend on this fire, and that when it goes out, the person dies.
teachings.link: Science found something close. Your cells set free the energy in food with oxygen, the same change as in a flame, only slower. The old healers had no microscopes, so this is a parallel, not a proof.

teachings.teaching: The Greek thinker Heraclitus, about 2,500 years ago, said the world is an ever-living fire, always being lit and going out in measures, yet keeping its pattern.
teachings.link: A flame keeps its shape while new wax and air pass through it. Your body keeps its shape while food and air pass through it, and its warmth comes from the same kind of change as a flame's.

teachings.teaching: The hymn of creation asks how everything began, and ends with an honest question: perhaps even the one who watches from the highest heaven does not know.
teachings.link: Scientists still do not know how the first life came from non-living chemicals. Saying 'we do not know' is part of being honest.

science.text: Respiration in cells and burning both join fuel with oxygen and give out carbon dioxide, water and energy. Cells do it in many small steps, each one helped along by a protein called an enzyme.
Living things are made of the same kinds of atoms as non-living things, and most of those atoms were made in stars.

other_view.view: The chemistry is shared, but life is still a real difference in nature, not only a word. Only living things have cells and pass on instructions, and fire and crystals really lack them. Most scientists also think awareness needs a living brain and nerves. In ancient India, the Charvaka school said there is only matter, and that awareness ends with the body.

practice.title: The fire inside
practice.say: Sit comfortably and close your eyes. Rub your palms together, then put them on your cheeks. Feel how warm you are. Now breathe out slowly onto the back of your hand. Feel the warm, damp air. Take ten slow breaths, and count them on your fingers. With each breath in, oxygen goes to your cells. With each breath out, carbon dioxide and water leave. Open your eyes. Where in you is the fire?
practice.kid: Close your eyes. Put your hands on your cheeks. Feel how warm you are. Breathe out on your hand. Feel the warm, damp air. Take ten slow breaths. Where in you is the fire?

ask: Your body is warm and a flame is hot, for almost the same reason. So what is the real difference between you and a flame?
If life uses the same chemistry as fire, what makes a dry seed alive and a flame not?
Biologists say fire is not alive. Could something be not alive and still be aware in its own way?
Is there anything in the world that is completely not alive? How could you be sure?
roots.art: A child sitting beside a lit diya with palms on their cheeks. Arrows show food and air going into the child and warmth and breath coming out, matching arrows of oil and air going into the flame and warmth and smoke coming out.

how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, people thought that when something burns, it gives off a hidden substance called phlogiston. A candle in a closed jar went out, they said, because the air had filled up with phlogiston. In the 1770s, the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier weighed things carefully before and after burning. Metals got heavier when they burned, not lighter. So burning was not losing something. It was joining with a part of the air, which Lavoisier named oxygen. Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier worked beside him. She translated English papers for him, kept records and drew the equipment. Then Lavoisier asked whether breathing was the same. In 1782 and 1783, with Pierre-Simon Laplace, he put a guinea pig in a box packed with ice, and measured how much ice their body heat melted. He compared this with burning charcoal that made the same amount of carbon dioxide. The two amounts of heat were close. So breathing is a slow burning. Lavoisier thought this burning happened in the lungs. About a hundred years later, scientists showed that it happens inside every cell.
how_we_found_out.who: Antoine Lavoisier and Marie-Anne Paulze Lavoisier, with Pierre-Simon Laplace
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That burning gives off a hidden substance called phlogiston. Weighing showed that burning metals get heavier, because they join with oxygen from the air. Lavoisier's own wrong idea, that breathing burns food in the lungs, was corrected later: it happens in every cell.
